**Harry S. Truman**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-2) (May 8, 1884–December 26, 1972) was the 33rd [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"), serving from 1945 to 1953. As the 34th [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_president_of_the_United_States "Vice president of the United States") in 1945, he assumed the presidency upon the death of [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") in April. Truman set up the [Marshall Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Plan "Marshall Plan") to rebuild the badly damaged economy of Western Europe. He established the [Truman Doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truman_Doctrine "Truman Doctrine") and supported the founding of [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") to contain the expansion of [Soviet communism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_communism "Soviet communism"). A member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Democratic_Party_(United_States) "History of the Democratic Party (United States)"), he proposed numerous [New Deal coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal_coalition "New Deal coalition") liberal domestic reforms, but few were enacted by the [conservative coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_coalition "Conservative coalition") that dominated the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress").

Born in rural Missouri, Truman was raised in [Independence, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence,_Missouri "Independence, Missouri"), and during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), he fought in France as a captain in the Field Artillery. Returning home, he opened a [haberdashery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haberdasher "Haberdasher") in [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri"), and was elected as a judge of [Jackson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Missouri "Jackson County, Missouri") in 1922. Truman was elected to the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate") for Missouri in 1934. Between 1940 and 1944, he gained national prominence as the chairman of the [Truman Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truman_Committee "Truman Committee"), which aimed to reduce waste and inefficiency in wartime contracts. Truman was elected vice president in the [1944 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1944_United_States_presidential_election "1944 United States presidential election") and became president upon Roosevelt's death in April 1945. Only then was he told about the ongoing [Manhattan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project") and the [atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb"). Truman authorized the [first and only use of nuclear weapons in war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki "Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki") against the Japanese cities of [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima") and [Nagasaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagasaki "Nagasaki").

[Truman's administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Harry_S._Truman "Presidency of Harry S. Truman") engaged in an [internationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationalism_(politics) "Internationalism (politics)") foreign policy by [working closely with Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Relationship#Attlee_and_Truman_(July_1945_%E2%80%93_October_1951) "Special Relationship"). Truman staunchly denounced [isolationism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isolationism "Isolationism"). He energized the [New Deal coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal_coalition "New Deal coalition") during the [1948 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_United_States_presidential_election "1948 United States presidential election"), despite some Democrats splitting off into the [Dixiecrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixiecrats "Dixiecrats"), and defeated both the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") nominee [Thomas E. Dewey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_E._Dewey "Thomas E. Dewey") and Dixiecrat [Strom Thurmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strom_Thurmond "Strom Thurmond"). Truman presided over the onset of the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") in 1947. He oversaw the [Berlin Airlift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Airlift "Berlin Airlift") and the Marshall Plan in 1948. With America's involvement in the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War") (1950–1953), [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea") repelled the invasion by [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"). Domestically, the postwar economic challenges such as strikes and inflation created a mixed reaction over the effectiveness of his administration. In 1948, he proposed that Congress should pass comprehensive civil rights legislation. Congress refused, so Truman issued Executive Order 9980 and [Executive Order 9981](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_9981 "Executive Order 9981"), which prohibited discrimination in agencies of [the federal government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") and desegregated the [United States Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Armed_Forces "United States Armed Forces").

Investigations revealed [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption_in_the_United_States "Corruption in the United States") in parts of the Truman administration, and this became a major campaign issue in the [1952 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_United_States_presidential_election "1952 United States presidential election"), although they did not implicate Truman himself. He was eligible for reelection in 1952 but he chose not to run due to poor polling. Subsequently, Truman went into a retirement marked by the founding of [his presidential library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman_Presidential_Library_and_Museum "Harry S. Truman Presidential Library and Museum") and the publication of his memoirs. It was long believed that Truman's retirement years were financially difficult, resulting in Congress establishing a pension for former presidents. However, evidence eventually emerged that he amassed considerable wealth, some of it during his presidency. When Truman left office, his administration was heavily criticized. Despite this controversy, historians consistently [rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States "Historical rankings of presidents of the United States") Truman in the first quartile of U.S. presidents. In addition, critical reassessments of his presidency have improved his reputation among historians and the general population.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-3)

## Early life, family, and education

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Harry_ca._1897.jpg/250px-Harry_ca._1897.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harry_ca._1897.jpg)

Truman at age 13 in 1897

Harry S. Truman was born in [Lamar, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamar,_Missouri "Lamar, Missouri"), on May 8, 1884, the oldest child of John Anderson Truman and [Martha Ellen Young Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Ellen_Young_Truman "Martha Ellen Young Truman"). He was named for his maternal uncle, Harrison "Harry" Young. His middle initial, "S", is not an abbreviation of one particular name. Rather, it honors both his grandfathers, Anderson Shipp Truman and Solomon Young, a somewhat common practice in the [American South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_South "American South") at the time.[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-5)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough199237-6) A brother, John Vivian, was born soon after Harry, followed by sister Mary Jane.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough199227,_37-7) While Truman's ancestry was primarily [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Americans "English Americans"), he also had some [Scots-Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scots-Irish_Americans "Scots-Irish Americans"), [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Americans "German Americans"), and [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Americans "French Americans") ancestry.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-8)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-9)

John Truman was a farmer and livestock dealer. The family lived in Lamar until Harry was ten months old, when they moved to a farm near [Harrisonville, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrisonville,_Missouri "Harrisonville, Missouri"). They next moved to [Belton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belton,_Missouri "Belton, Missouri") and in 1887 to his grandparents' 600-acre (240 ha) farm in [Grandview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandview,_Missouri "Grandview, Missouri").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTETruman_Library,_Birth2012-10) When Truman was six, his parents moved to [Independence, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence,_Missouri "Independence, Missouri"), so he could attend the [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian") Church Sunday School. He did not attend a conventional school until he was eight years old.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough199237,_77,_1112-11) While living in Independence, he served as a [Shabbos goy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabbos_goy "Shabbos goy") for Jewish neighbors, doing tasks for them on [Shabbat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabbat "Shabbat") that their religion prevented them from doing on that day.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-12)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-13)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-14)

Truman was interested in music, reading, history, and mathematics,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-15) all encouraged by his mother, with whom he was very close. As president, he solicited political as well as personal advice from her.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOshinsky2004365%E2%80%93380-16) Truman learned to play the [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano") at age seven and took lessons from Mrs. E.C. White, a well-respected teacher in [Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough199252-17) He got up at five o'clock every morning to practice the piano, which he studied more than twice a week until he was fifteen, becoming quite a skilled player.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough199238-18) During the [1900 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Democratic_National_Convention "1900 Democratic National Convention") in Kansas City, Truman served as a page.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrell199487-19) His father, a dedicated Democrat, had numerous friends involved in the [Missouri state Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Democratic_Party "Missouri Democratic Party"), which helped young Harry secure his first political position. At the convention, Truman witnessed a speech by the party's nominee for [that year's presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_United_States_presidential_election "1900 United States presidential election"), [William Jennings Bryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan "William Jennings Bryan"), who would later become his political hero.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTETruman_Library2012aa-20)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-21)

After graduating from [Independence High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Chrisman_High_School "William Chrisman High School") in 1901,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-22) Truman took classes at Spalding's Commercial College, a Kansas City business school. He studied bookkeeping, shorthand, and typing but stopped after a year.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrell199425%E2%80%9326-23)

[Segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States "Racial segregation in the United States") was practiced and largely accepted where Truman grew up. While he later came to support civil rights, early letters of the young Truman reflected his upbringing and prejudices against [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans"), [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews") and [Asian Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Americans "Asian Americans").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-24)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-25)

## Working career

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Trumanhist.JPG/250px-Trumanhist.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trumanhist.JPG)

[Truman's home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman_National_Historic_Site "Harry S. Truman National Historic Site") in [Independence, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence,_Missouri "Independence, Missouri")

Truman was employed briefly in the mailroom of _[The Kansas City Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kansas\_City\_Star "The Kansas City Star")_[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-26) before making use of his business college experience to obtain a job as a timekeeper for construction crews on the [Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atchison,_Topeka_and_Santa_Fe_Railway "Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway"), which required him to sleep in workmen's camps along the rail lines.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTETruman_Library,_Job2012-27) Truman and his brother Vivian later worked as clerks at the [National Bank of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Bank_of_Commerce_(Kansas_City) "National Bank of Commerce (Kansas City)") in Kansas City.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-28)

In 1906, Truman returned to the Grandview farm, where he lived until entering the army in 1917.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough199267,_99-29) During this period, he courted [Bess Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bess_Wallace "Bess Wallace").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-30) He proposed in 1911, but she turned him down.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeselbracht-31) Believing Wallace turned him down because he did not have much money, Truman later said he intended to propose again, but he wanted to have a better income than that earned by a farmer.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough199278%E2%80%9379-32) In fact, Wallace later told Truman she did not intend to marry, but if she did, it would be to him.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeselbracht-31) Still determined to improve his finances, during his years on the farm and immediately after World War I, Truman became active in several business ventures. These included a lead and zinc mine near [Commerce, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commerce,_Oklahoma "Commerce, Oklahoma"), a company that bought land and leased the oil drilling rights to prospectors, and speculation in Kansas City real estate.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrell199452,_53,_79-33) Truman occasionally derived some income from these enterprises, but none proved successful in the long term.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-34)

Truman is the only president since [William McKinley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_McKinley "William McKinley") (elected in 1896) who did not earn a college degree.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-35) In addition to having briefly attended business college, from 1923 to 1925 he took night courses toward an [LL.B.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LL.B. "LL.B.") at the Kansas City Law School (now the [University of Missouri–Kansas City School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Missouri%E2%80%93Kansas_City_School_of_Law "University of Missouri–Kansas City School of Law")) but dropped out after losing reelection as county judge.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHamby199517%E2%80%9318,_135-36) He was informed by attorneys in the Kansas City area that his education and experience were probably sufficient to receive a license to practice law but did not pursue it because he won election as presiding judge.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-37)

While serving as president in 1947, Truman applied for a law license.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-38) A friend who was an attorney began working out the arrangements, and informed Truman that his application had to be notarized. By the time Truman received this information he had changed his mind, so he never followed up. After the discovery of Truman's application in 1996 the [Missouri Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Supreme_Court "Missouri Supreme Court") issued him a posthumous honorary law license.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-39)

## Military service

### National Guard

Due to the lack of funds for college, Truman considered attending the [United States Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy "United States Military Academy") at [West Point, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point,_New_York "West Point, New York"), which had no tuition, but he was refused an appointment because of poor eyesight.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHamby199517%E2%80%9318,_135-36) He enlisted in the [Missouri National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_National_Guard "Missouri National Guard") in 1905 and served until 1911 in the Kansas City-based [Battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery_battery "Artillery battery") B, 2nd Missouri Field Artillery Regiment, in which he attained the rank of [corporal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal#United_States "Corporal").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilwee2000-40) At his induction, his eyesight without glasses was unacceptable: [20/50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_acuity "Visual acuity") in the right eye and 20/400 in the left (past the standard for legal blindness).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992105-41) The second time he took the test, he passed by secretly memorizing the eye chart.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTETruman_Library,_Eye2012-42) He was described as 5 feet 10 inches (178 cm) tall, [gray eyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gray_eyed "Gray eyed"), dark haired and of light complexion.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-43)

### World War I

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Harry_S._Truman_in_his_World_War_I_Army_uniform.jpg/250px-Harry_S._Truman_in_his_World_War_I_Army_uniform.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harry_S._Truman_in_his_World_War_I_Army_uniform.jpg)

Truman in September 1917

When the United States entered [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") on [April 6, 1917](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_entry_into_World_War_I "American entry into World War I"), Truman rejoined Battery B, successfully recruiting new soldiers for the expanding unit, for which he was elected as their [first lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_lieutenant#U.S._Army,_U.S._Marine_Corps_and_U.S._Air_Force "First lieutenant").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-44) Before deployment to France, Truman was sent for training to [Camp Doniphan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Doniphan,_Oklahoma "Camp Doniphan, Oklahoma"), [Fort Sill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Sill "Fort Sill"), near [Lawton, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawton,_Oklahoma "Lawton, Oklahoma"), when his regiment was federalized as the [129th Field Artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/129th_Field_Artillery "129th Field Artillery").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-45) The regimental commander during its training was [Robert M. Danford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_M._Danford "Robert M. Danford"), who later served as the Army's Chief of Field Artillery.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Another_Such_Victory''6-46) Truman recalled that he learned more practical, useful information from Danford in six weeks than from six months of formal Army instruction, and when Truman served as an artillery instructor, he consciously patterned his approach on Danford's.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Another_Such_Victory''6-46)

Truman also ran the camp [canteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_exchange "Post exchange") with [Edward Jacobson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Jacobson "Edward Jacobson"), a clothing store clerk he knew from Kansas City. Unlike most canteens funded by unit members, which usually lost money, the canteen operated by Truman and Jacobson turned a profit, returning each soldier's initial $2 investment and $10,000 in dividends in six months.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilwee2000-40) At Fort Sill, Truman met Lieutenant James M. Pendergast, nephew of [Tom Pendergast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Pendergast "Tom Pendergast"), a Kansas City political boss, a connection that had a profound influence on Truman's later life.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992105%E2%80%93110-47)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-48)

In mid-1918, about one million soldiers of the [American Expeditionary Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Expeditionary_Forces "American Expeditionary Forces") (AEF) were in France.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurrentFreidelWilliams1971594-49) Truman was promoted to [captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States_O-3) "Captain (United States O-3)") effective April 23,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-50) and in July became commander of the newly arrived Battery D, 129th Field Artillery, [35th Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/35th_Infantry_Division_(United_States) "35th Infantry Division (United States)").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992115-51)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-52) Battery D was known for its discipline problems, and Truman was initially unpopular because of his efforts to restore order.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilwee2000-40) Despite attempts by the men to intimidate him into quitting, Truman succeeded by making his corporals and sergeants accountable for discipline. He promised to back them up if they performed capably and reduce them to private if they did not.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurnes200349-53) In an event memorialized in battery lore as "The Battle of Who Run", his soldiers began to flee during a sudden night attack by the Germans in the [Vosges Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vosges_Mountains "Vosges Mountains"); Truman succeeded at ordering his men to stay and fight, using profanity from his railroad days. The men were so surprised to hear Truman use such language that they immediately obeyed.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilwee2000-40)

Truman's unit joined in a massive prearranged assault barrage on September 26, 1918, at the opening of the [Meuse–Argonne offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meuse%E2%80%93Argonne_offensive "Meuse–Argonne offensive").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-Farinacci-54) They advanced with difficulty over [pitted terrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zone_rouge "Zone rouge") to follow the infantry, and set up an observation post west of [Cheppy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheppy "Cheppy").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-Farinacci-54) On September 27, Truman saw through his binoculars an enemy artillery battery deploying across a river in a position which would allow them to fire upon the neighboring [28th Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/28th_Division_(United_States) "28th Division (United States)").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-Farinacci-54) Truman's orders limited him to targets facing the 35th Division, but he ignored this and patiently waited until the Germans had walked their horses well away from their guns, ensuring they could not relocate out of range of Truman's battery.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-Farinacci-54) He then ordered his men to open fire, and their attack destroyed the enemy battery.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-Farinacci-54) His actions were credited with saving the lives of 28th Division soldiers who otherwise would have come under fire from the Germans.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992130,_531-55)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiangreco2002192-56) Truman was given a dressing down by his regimental commander, Colonel Karl D. Klemm, who threatened to convene a court-martial, but Klemm never followed through, and Truman was not punished.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-Farinacci-54)

[![Image 13: Truman in military uniform with shoulder and waist belt with helmet](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Harry_S._Truman_WW_I.jpg/250px-Harry_S._Truman_WW_I.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harry_S._Truman_WW_I.jpg)

Truman in uniform, c. 1918

In other action during the Meuse–Argonne offensive, Truman's battery provided support for [George S. Patton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_S._Patton "George S. Patton")'s tank brigade,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiangreco2002181%E2%80%93186-57) and fired some of the last shots of the war on November 11, 1918. Battery D did not lose any men while under Truman's command in France. To show their appreciation for his leadership, his men presented him with a large [loving cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loving_cup "Loving cup") upon their return to the United States after the war.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilwee2000-40)

The war was a transformative experience in which Truman manifested his leadership qualities. He had entered the service in 1917 as a family farmer who had worked in clerical jobs that did not require the ability to motivate and direct others, but during the war, he gained leadership experience and a record of success that greatly enhanced and supported his post-war political career in Missouri.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilwee2000-40)

Truman was brought up in the Presbyterian and [Baptist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptist "Baptist") churches,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-58) but avoided [revivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revival_meeting "Revival meeting") and sometimes ridiculed revivalist preachers.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-59) He rarely spoke about religion, which to him, primarily meant ethical behavior along traditional Protestant lines.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-60) Truman once wrote in a letter to his future wife, Bess: "You know that I know nothing about Lent and such things..."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-61) Most of the soldiers he commanded in the war were Catholics, and one of his close friends was the 129th Field Artillery's chaplain, [Monsignor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsignor "Monsignor") L. Curtis Tiernan.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-62) The two remained friends until Tiernan's death in 1960.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%22Biographical_Sketch,_L._Curtis_Tiernan%22-63) Developing leadership and interpersonal skills that later made him a successful politician helped Truman get along with his Catholic soldiers, as he did with soldiers of other Christian denominations and the unit's Jewish members.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-64)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-65)

### Officers' Reserve Corps

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Officers%2C_129th_Field_Artillery%2C_at_regimental_headquarters_at_Ch%C3%A2teau_du_Chesnay_near_Courcemont%2C_France%2C_March_1919._Cap_-_NARA_-_530949.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Officers%2C_129th_Field_Artillery%2C_at_regimental_headquarters_at_Ch%C3%A2teau_du_Chesnay_near_Courcemont%2C_France%2C_March_1919._Cap_-_NARA_-_530949.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Officers,_129th_Field_Artillery,_at_regimental_headquarters_at_Ch%C3%A2teau_du_Chesnay_near_Courcemont,_France,_March_1919._Cap_-_NARA_-_530949.tif)

Officers of the 129th Field Artillery, at regimental headquarters at Chateau le Chanay near Courcemont, France, March 1919. Captain Harry S. Truman is pictured in the second row, third from the right.

Truman was honorably discharged from the Army as a [captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States_O-3) "Captain (United States O-3)") on May 6, 1919.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-66) In 1920, he was appointed a [major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_(United_States) "Major (United States)") in the [Officers Reserve Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officers_Reserve_Corps "Officers Reserve Corps").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-67) He became a [lieutenant colonel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Colonel_(United_States) "Lieutenant Colonel (United States)") in 1925 and a [colonel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel_(United_States) "Colonel (United States)") in 1932.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-68) In the 1920s and 1930s he commanded 1st Battalion, 379th Field Artillery Regiment, [102nd Infantry Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/102nd_Infantry_Division_(United_States) "102nd Infantry Division (United States)").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-69) After promotion to colonel, Truman advanced to command of the regiment.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-70)

After his election to the U.S. Senate, Truman was transferred to the General Assignments Group, a holding unit for less active officers, although he had not been consulted in advance.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-ReferenceA-71) Truman protested his reassignment, which led to his resumption of regimental command.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-ReferenceA-71) He remained an active reservist until the early 1940s.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-72) Truman volunteered for active military service during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), but was not accepted, partly because of age, and partly because President [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") desired that senators and congressmen who belonged to the military reserves support the war effort by remaining in Congress, or by ending their active duty service and resuming their congressional seats.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-73) He was an inactive reservist from the early 1940s until retiring as a colonel in the then redesignated [U.S. Army Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Reserve "U.S. Army Reserve") on January 20, 1953.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-74)

### Military awards and decorations

Truman was awarded a [World War I Victory Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I_Victory_Medal_(United_States) "World War I Victory Medal (United States)") with two [battle clasps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_clasps "Battle clasps") (for [St. Mihiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Saint-Mihiel "Battle of Saint-Mihiel") and [Meuse-Argonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meuse-Argonne "Meuse-Argonne")) and a [Defensive Sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Front_(World_War_I) "Western Front (World War I)") Clasp. He was also the recipient of two [Armed Forces Reserve Medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_Reserve_Medal "Armed Forces Reserve Medal").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-75) After the war, Truman almost always wore a bronze World War I victory lapel pin as a memento of his overseas service.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-76)

## After the War

### Marriage

[![Image 15: Wedding photo of Truman in gray suit and his wife in hat with white dress holding flowers](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/TrumanWedding.PNG/250px-TrumanWedding.PNG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TrumanWedding.PNG)

Harry and Bess Truman on their wedding day, June 28, 1919

After his wartime service, Truman returned to Independence, where he married Bess Wallace on June 28, 1919.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTETruman_Library1919-77) The couple had one child, [Mary Margaret Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Margaret_Truman "Mary Margaret Truman").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldstein2008-78)

Shortly before the wedding, Truman and Jacobson opened a [haberdashery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haberdashery "Haberdashery") together at 104 West 12th Street in downtown [Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992146,_151%E2%80%93152-79) After brief initial success, the store went bankrupt during the [recession of 1921](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-World_War_I_recession "Post-World War I recession").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOshinsky2004365%E2%80%93380-16) Truman did not pay off the last of the debts from that venture until 1935, when he did so with the aid of banker [William T. Kemper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_T._Kemper "William T. Kemper"), who worked behind the scenes to enable Truman's brother Vivian to buy Truman's $5,600 [promissory note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loan_agreement "Loan agreement") during the asset sale of a bank that had failed in the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough199263%E2%80%9364,_68-80)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrell199488-81) The note had risen and fallen in value as it was bought and sold, interest accumulated and Truman made payments, so by the time the last bank to hold it failed, it was worth nearly $9,000.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrell199486-82) Thanks to Kemper's efforts, Vivian Truman was able to buy it for $1,000.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrell199488-81) Jacobson and Truman remained close friends even after their store failed, and Jacobson's advice to Truman on [Zionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zionism "Zionism") later played a role in the U.S. Government's decision to recognize Israel.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHamby1995410%E2%80%93412-83)

### Jackson County judge

With the help of the Kansas City [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)")[machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_machine "Political machine") led by [Tom Pendergast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Pendergast "Tom Pendergast"), Truman was elected in 1922 as County Court judge of [Jackson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Missouri "Jackson County, Missouri")'s eastern district—Jackson County's three-judge court included judges from the western district (Kansas City), the eastern district (the county outside Kansas City), and a presiding judge elected countywide. This was an administrative rather than a judicial court, similar to [county commissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_commission "County commission") in many other jurisdictions. Truman succeeded James E. Gilday and served from January 1, 1923, to January 1, 1925.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-84) He lost his 1924 reelection campaign to Henry Rummel in a Republican wave led by President [Calvin Coolidge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Coolidge "Calvin Coolidge")'s [landslide election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1924_United_States_presidential_election "1924 United States presidential election") to a full term.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%22County_Judges_1923%E2%80%931972%22-85) Two years selling automobile club memberships convinced him that a public service career was safer for a family man approaching middle age, and he planned a run for [presiding judge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_county_executives_of_Jackson_County,_Missouri "List of county executives of Jackson County, Missouri") in 1926.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek20086-86)

Truman won the job in 1926 with the support of the Pendergast machine, and succeeded Elihu W. Hayes.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-87) Truman was re-elected in 1930; he served from January 1, 1927, to January 1, 1935, and was succeeded by Eugene I. Purcell.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%22County_Judges_1923%E2%80%931972%22-85) As presiding judge, Truman helped coordinate the _Ten Year Plan_, which transformed Jackson County and the Kansas City skyline with new public works projects, including an extensive series of roads and construction of a new [Wight and Wight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wight_and_Wight "Wight and Wight")-designed [County Court building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County_Courthouse_(Kansas_City,_Missouri) "Jackson County Courthouse (Kansas City, Missouri)"). Also in 1926, he became president of the [National Old Trails Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Old_Trails_Road "National Old Trails Road") Association, and during his term he oversaw dedication of 12 [Madonna of the Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna_of_the_Trail "Madonna of the Trail") monuments to honor pioneer women.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek20086-86)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarr2004-88)

In 1933, Truman was named Missouri's director for the Federal Re-Employment program (part of the [Civil Works Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Works_Administration "Civil Works Administration")) at the request of Postmaster General [James Farley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Farley "James Farley"). This was payback to Pendergast for delivering the Kansas City vote to [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") in the [1932 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_United_States_presidential_election "1932 United States presidential election"). The appointment confirmed Pendergast's control over federal [patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage") jobs in Missouri and marked the zenith of his power. It also created a relationship between Truman and Roosevelt's aide [Harry Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Hopkins "Harry Hopkins") and assured Truman's avid support for the New Deal.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTESavage199165-89)

### U.S. Senator from Missouri

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Truman_campaigning_in_1934.jpg/250px-Truman_campaigning_in_1934.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Truman_campaigning_in_1934.jpg)

Truman campaigning in [Thayer, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thayer,_Missouri "Thayer, Missouri"), c.October 5, 1934

After serving as a county judge, Truman wanted to run for [governor of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Missouri "Governor of Missouri") or [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress"),[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-90)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-Collector-91) but Pendergast rejected these ideas. Truman then thought he might serve out his career in some well-paying county sinecure;[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-Collector-91) circumstances changed when Pendergast reluctantly backed him as the machine's choice in the 1934 Democratic [primary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_election "Primary election") for the [U.S. Senate from Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1934_United_States_Senate_election_in_Missouri "1934 United States Senate election in Missouri"), after Pendergast's first four choices had declined to run.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUnited_States_Senate2012-92)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-95) In the primary, Truman defeated Congressmen [John J. Cochran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_J._Cochran "John J. Cochran") and [Jacob L. Milligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_L._Milligan "Jacob L. Milligan") with the solid support of [Jackson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Missouri "Jackson County, Missouri"), which was crucial to his candidacy. Also critical were the contacts he had made statewide in his capacity as a county official, member of the [Freemasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freemasons "Freemasons"),[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-97) military reservist,[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-99) and member of the American Legion.[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-101)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKirkendall198927-102) In the general election, Truman defeated incumbent Republican [Roscoe C. Patterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe_C._Patterson "Roscoe C. Patterson") by nearly 20 percentage points in a continuing wave of pro-[New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal "New Deal") Democrats elected during the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression_in_the_United_States "Great Depression in the United States").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUnited_States_Senate2012-92)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek20087%E2%80%939-103)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinn-104)

Truman assumed office with a reputation as "the Senator from Pendergast". He referred patronage decisions to Pendergast but maintained that he voted with his own conscience. He later defended the patronage decisions by saying that "by offering a little to the machine, [he] saved a lot".[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinn-104)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Time''January_8,_1973-105) In his first term, Truman spoke out against corporate greed and the dangers of [Wall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street "Wall Street") speculators and other moneyed special interests attaining too much influence in national affairs.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992232-106) Though he served on the high-profile [Appropriations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Appropriations "United States Senate Committee on Appropriations") and [Interstate Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Commerce,_Science,_and_Transportation#Committee_on_Aeronautical_and_Space_Sciences,_1958-1977 "United States Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation") Committees, he was largely ignored by President Roosevelt and had trouble getting calls returned from the White House.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinn-104)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992230-107)

During the [U.S. Senate election in 1940](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1940_United_States_Senate_election_in_Missouri "1940 United States Senate election in Missouri"), U.S. Attorney [Maurice Milligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Milligan "Maurice Milligan") (former opponent Jacob Milligan's brother) and former governor [Lloyd Stark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Stark "Lloyd Stark") both challenged Truman in the Democratic primary. Truman was politically weakened by Pendergast's imprisonment for income tax evasion the previous year; the senator had remained loyal, having claimed that Republican judges (not the Roosevelt administration) were responsible for the boss's downfall.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek200811%E2%80%9312-108)[St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis") party leader [Robert E. Hannegan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Hannegan "Robert E. Hannegan")'s support of Truman proved crucial; he later brokered the deal that put Truman on the national ticket. In the end, Stark and Milligan split the anti-Pendergast vote in the Senate Democratic primary and Truman won by a total of 8,000 votes. In the November election, Truman defeated Republican [Manvel H. Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manvel_H._Davis "Manvel H. Davis") by 51–49 percent.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHamby1995236%E2%80%93247-109) As senator, Truman opposed both Nazi Germany and Communist Russia. Two days after [Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany_invaded_the_Soviet_Union "Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union") in June 1941, Truman said:

> If we see that Germany is winning we ought to help Russia, and if Russia is winning we ought to help Germany, and that way let them kill as many as possible although I don't want to see [Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hitler "Hitler") victorious under any circumstances.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-110)

This quote without its last part later became a staple in [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propaganda_in_the_Soviet_Union "Propaganda in the Soviet Union") and later [Russian propaganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_propaganda "Russian propaganda") as "evidence" of an American conspiracy to destroy the country.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-111)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-112)

#### Truman Committee

Further information: [Truman Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truman_Committee "Truman Committee")

In late 1940, Truman traveled to various military bases. The waste and profiteering he saw led him to use his chairmanship of the [Committee on Military Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Armed_Services#Committee_on_Military_Affairs,_1816%E2%80%931947 "United States Senate Committee on Armed Services") Subcommittee on War Mobilization to start investigations into abuses while the nation prepared for war. A new special committee was set up under Truman to conduct a formal investigation; the White House supported this plan rather than weather a more hostile probe by the House of Representatives. The main mission of the committee was to expose and fight waste and corruption in the gigantic government wartime contracts.

Truman's initiative convinced Senate leaders of the necessity for the committee, which reflected his demands for honest and efficient administration and his distrust of big business and Wall Street. Truman managed the committee "with extraordinary skill" and usually achieved consensus, generating heavy media publicity that gave him a national reputation.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-113)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek200812%E2%80%9314-114) Activities of the Truman Committee ranged from criticizing the "[dollar-a-year men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar-a-year_men "Dollar-a-year men")" hired by the government, many of whom proved ineffective, to investigating a shoddily built New Jersey housing project for war workers.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-115)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Life''November_30,_1942-116) In March 1944, Truman attempted to probe the expensive [Manhattan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project") but was persuaded by Secretary of War [Henry L. Stimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_L._Stimson "Henry L. Stimson") to discontinue with the investigation.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-zuberi2001-117):634

## Vice presidency (1945)

See also: [1944 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1944_Democratic_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection "1944 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection")

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Truman-Mother-LIFE-1944.jpg/250px-Truman-Mother-LIFE-1944.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Truman-Mother-LIFE-1944.jpg)

Truman visits [his mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Ellen_Young_Truman "Martha Ellen Young Truman") in [Grandview, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandview,_Missouri "Grandview, Missouri"), after being [nominated the Democratic candidate for vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_vice_presidential_nomination_of_1944 "Democratic vice presidential nomination of 1944"), July 1944.

[![Image 18: election poster from 1944 with Roosevelt and Truman](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/RooseveltTruman1944poster.jpg/250px-RooseveltTruman1944poster.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RooseveltTruman1944poster.jpg)

[Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt")–Truman poster from [1944](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1944_United_States_presidential_election "1944 United States presidential election")

Roosevelt's advisors knew that Roosevelt might not live out a fourth term and that his vice president would very likely become the next president. [Henry A. Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Wallace "Henry A. Wallace") had served as Roosevelt's vice president for four years and was popular on the left, but he was viewed as too far to the left and too friendly to labor for some of Roosevelt's advisers. The President and several of his confidantes wanted to replace Wallace with someone more acceptable to Democratic Party leaders. Outgoing Democratic National Committee chairman [Frank C. Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_C._Walker "Frank C. Walker"), incoming chairman Hannegan, party treasurer [Edwin W. Pauley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_W._Pauley "Edwin W. Pauley"), Bronx party boss [Ed Flynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_J._Flynn "Edward J. Flynn"), Chicago Mayor [Edward Joseph Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Joseph_Kelly "Edward Joseph Kelly"), and lobbyist George E. Allen all wanted to keep Wallace off the ticket.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992373%E2%80%93378-124) Roosevelt told party leaders that he would accept either Truman or Supreme Court Justice [William O. Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_O._Douglas "William O. Douglas").[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-125)

State and city party leaders strongly preferred Truman, and Roosevelt agreed.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurnes2003131-126) Truman had repeatedly said that he was not in the race and that he did not want the vice presidency, and he remained reluctant.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurnes2003131-126) One reason was that his wife and sister Mary Jane were both on his Senate staff payroll, and he feared negative publicity.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurnes2003131-126) Truman did not campaign for the vice-presidential spot, though he welcomed the attention as evidence that he had become more than the "Senator from Pendergast".[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek200814%E2%80%9316-127) Truman's nomination was dubbed the "Second [Missouri Compromise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Compromise "Missouri Compromise")" and was well received. The Roosevelt–Truman ticket achieved a 432–99[electoral-vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College") victory in the election, defeating the Republican ticket of Governor [Thomas E. Dewey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_E._Dewey "Thomas E. Dewey") of New York and running mate Governor [John Bricker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bricker "John Bricker") of Ohio. Truman was [sworn in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_inauguration_of_Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Fourth inauguration of Franklin D. Roosevelt") as vice president on January 20, 1945.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek200815%E2%80%9317-128) After the inauguration, Truman called his mother, who instructed him, "Now you behave yourself."[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-129)

Truman's brief vice-presidency was relatively uneventful. Truman mostly presided over the Senate and attended parties and receptions. He kept the same offices from his Senate years, mostly using the Vice President's official office in the Capitol only to greet visitors. Truman was the first vice president to have a Secret Service agent assigned to him. Truman envisioned the office as a liaison between the Senate and the president.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992333%E2%80%93336-130) On April 10, 1945,[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-131) Truman cast his only [tie-breaking vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tie-breaking_votes_cast_by_the_vice_president_of_the_United_States "List of tie-breaking votes cast by the vice president of the United States") as president of the Senate, against a [Robert A. Taft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_A._Taft "Robert A. Taft") amendment that would have blocked the postwar delivery of [Lend-Lease Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lend-Lease_Act "Lend-Lease Act") items contracted for during the war.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-132)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-133) Roosevelt rarely contacted him, even to inform him of major decisions; the president and vice president met alone together only twice during their time in office.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallek200816-134)

In one of his first acts as vice president, Truman created some controversy when he attended the disgraced Pendergast's funeral. He brushed aside the criticism, saying simply, "He was always my friend and I have always been his."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOshinsky2004365%E2%80%93380-16) He had rarely discussed world affairs or domestic politics with Roosevelt; he was uninformed about major initiatives relating to the war and the top-secret [Manhattan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project"), which was about to test the world's first atomic bomb.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEU.S._History2012-135) In an event that generated negative publicity for Truman, he was photographed with actress [Lauren Bacall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauren_Bacall "Lauren Bacall") sitting atop the piano at the [National Press Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Press_Club_(United_States) "National Press Club (United States)") as he played for soldiers.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-136)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Photograph_of_Harry_S._Truman_taking_the_oath_of_office_as_President_of_the_United_States_in_the_Cabinet_Room_of_the..._-_NARA_-_199062.jpg/250px-Photograph_of_Harry_S._Truman_taking_the_oath_of_office_as_President_of_the_United_States_in_the_Cabinet_Room_of_the..._-_NARA_-_199062.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Photograph_of_Harry_S._Truman_taking_the_oath_of_office_as_President_of_the_United_States_in_the_Cabinet_Room_of_the..._-_NARA_-_199062.jpg)

Vice President Truman was sworn in as president in the [Cabinet Room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_Room_(White_House) "Cabinet Room (White House)") at the White House a few hours after Roosevelt's death.

Truman had been vice president for 82 days when President Roosevelt died on April 12, 1945.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEU.S._History2012-135) Truman, presiding over the Senate, as usual, had just adjourned the session for the day and was preparing to have a drink in [House Speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives")[Sam Rayburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Rayburn "Sam Rayburn")'s [office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideaway_(U.S._Senate) "Hideaway (U.S. Senate)") when he received an urgent message to go immediately to the White House, where [Eleanor Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleanor_Roosevelt "Eleanor Roosevelt") told him that her husband had died after a massive [cerebral hemorrhage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_hemorrhage "Cerebral hemorrhage"). Truman asked her if there was anything he could do for her; she replied, "Is there anything we can do for _you_? For you are the one in trouble now!"[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTETruman_Library2012h-137)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992425-138)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodwin1994478-139) He was [sworn in as president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Harry_S._Truman "First inauguration of Harry S. Truman") at 7:09 p.m. in the West Wing of the White House, by Chief Justice [Harlan F. Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlan_F._Stone "Harlan F. Stone").[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-140)

## Presidency (1945–1953)

Main article: [Presidency of Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Harry_S._Truman "Presidency of Harry S. Truman")

Further information: [Foreign policy of the Harry S. Truman administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_Harry_S._Truman_administration "Foreign policy of the Harry S. Truman administration")

At the White House, Truman replaced Roosevelt holdovers with old confidants. The White House was badly understaffed with no more than a dozen aides; they could barely keep up with the heavy workflow of a greatly expanded executive department. Truman acted as his own [chief of staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Chief_of_Staff "White House Chief of Staff") on a daily basis, as well as his own liaison with Congress—a body he already knew very well. He was not well prepared to deal with the press, and never achieved the jovial familiarity of FDR. Filled with latent anger about all the setbacks in his career, he bitterly mistrusted journalists. He saw them as enemies lying in wait for his next careless miscue. Truman was a very hard worker, often to the point of exhaustion, which left him testy, easily annoyed, and on the verge of appearing unpresidential or petty. In terms of major issues, he discussed them in depth with top advisors. He mastered the details of the federal budget as well as anyone. Truman was a poor speaker reading a text. However, his visible anger made him an effective [stump speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stump_speaker "Stump speaker"), denouncing his enemies as his supporters hollered back at him "Give Em Hell, Harry!"[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-141)

Truman surrounded himself with friends and appointed several to high positions that seemed beyond their competence, including his two secretaries of the treasury, [Fred Vinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Vinson "Fred Vinson") and [John Snyder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wesley_Snyder_(US_Cabinet_Secretary) "John Wesley Snyder (US Cabinet Secretary)"). His closest friend in the White House was his military aide [Harry H. Vaughan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_H._Vaughan "Harry H. Vaughan"), who knew little of military or foreign affairs and was criticized for trading access to the White House for expensive gifts.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992366-142)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHamby1995301%E2%80%93302,_472-143) Truman loved to spend as much time as possible playing poker, telling stories and sipping bourbon. [Alonzo Hamby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonzo_Hamby "Alonzo Hamby") notes that:

> ... to many in the general public, gambling and bourbon swilling, however low-key, were not quite presidential. Neither was the intemperant "give 'em hell" campaign style nor the occasional profane phrase uttered in public. Poker exemplified a larger problem: the tension between his attempts at an image of leadership necessarily a cut above the ordinary and an informality that at times appeared to verge on crudeness.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHamby1995474-144)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCullough1992511-145)

# Celebrating Women's History in New York

Today is International Women’s Day — a great day to spotlight a few sites around New York that celebrate women who made history and helped shape our culture. This is an incomplete list and there are certainly so many more women whose stories went untold. But consider this a starting point if you are looking to do some exploring over the coming weeks and months and want to celebrate women’s history while you do.

* * *

## Shirley Chisholm State Park | Brooklyn

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CDuAm3uggsC/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Shirley Chisholm State Park (@shirleychisholmstatepark)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CDuAm3uggsC/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

Take advantage of a day with good weather and enjoy it outside while celebrating Shirley Chisholm, one of New York’s most iconic women. Chisholm was born in Brooklyn and represented her community in the House of Representatives from 1969-1983. She was the first African American woman elected to Congress, and in 1972, became the first African American candidate for a major party's presidential nomination, and the first woman to run for the Democratic Party's presidential nomination. The park honors her legacy with over 400 acres of land on the Brooklyn waterfront, complete with stunning views of the city and biking and hiking trails.

The park is open every day from 8:00 a.m.-dusk. [parks.ny.gov](https://parks.ny.gov/parks/200/details.aspx)

* * *

## Hilltop House and Studio | Cazenovia

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CMKKeyaL-hX/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Hilltop House And Studio (@hilltophouseandstudio)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CMKKeyaL-hX/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

At Stone Quarry Hill Art Park you will find the historic midcentury home and studio of artist Dorothy Riester and her husband Robert. [Hilltop House](https://www.preservenys.org/blog/voices-of-preservation-the-hilltop-house) and its grounds have been on the National Register of Historic Places since 2014, and in 2021 it was included into the [Historic Artists’ Homes and Studios program](https://artistshomes.org/). Dorothy Riester was an important woman artist working in the mid-twentieth century, and Hilltop House is a testament to her creativity and skill. The house was built in stages between the late 1950s-early 1970s and the interior was designed entirely by Riester. The architecture and the landscape are both deeply intertwined with Dorothy’s art. She was also a noted preservationist: “She founded a movement in Syracuse that successfully sponsored legislation aimed at preserving historic structures, and she was a founding member of the Cazenovia Preservation Foundation. Her preservation work continues with the open fields and wooded fringes of Stone Quarry Hill."

The grounds of the Art Park are open dawn to dusk every day. Tours of Hilltop House are currently postponed. [sqhap.org](https://sqhap.org/)

* * *

## NYC LGBT Historic Sites Walking Tours | NYC

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CL4RJEyBYeg/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by NYC LGBT HistoricSites Project (@nyclgbtsites)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CL4RJEyBYeg/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

Explore lesbian history in New York City courtesy of a curated walking tour from the NYC LGBT Historic Sites Project. [1970s Lesbian Activism & Community](https://www.nyclgbtsites.org/theme/1970s-lesbian-activism-community/) and [Lesbian Life Before Stonewall](https://www.nyclgbtsites.org/theme/lesbian-life-before-stonewall/) are particularly appropriate for Women’s History Month, but they have several [curated themes](https://www.nyclgbtsites.org/themes/) to choose from. Or, you could always choose your own adventure and [use their map to plot your own course](https://www.nyclgbtsites.org/) through the city. They have documented over 330 historic sites connected to New York City’s LGBT community, “giving life to its oft-untold history and influence on America.”

The NYC LGBT Historic Sites Project was one of our [Excellence in Historic Preservation Award winners in 2019](https://www.preservenys.org/blog/2019-excellence-award-winners).

* * *

## SANS | Sag Harbor

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CEXGUuFpHm5/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Preservation League of NYS (@preservenys)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CEXGUuFpHm5/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

Sag Harbor Hills, Azurest, and Ninevah Subdivisions (SANS) is a historically African American vacation community on Long Island. It was founded in 1947 by two sisters, Maude Terry and Amaza Lee Meredith, when they established Azurest (Sag Harbor Hills and Ninevah followed shortly after in 1950 and 1952, respectively). These two women negotiated the purchase and development of the land, and through their strong social networks found others to buy and construct houses on the 120 plots there. Amaza Lee Meredith is most well known for her [International-style home Azurest South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azurest_South), built on the campus of Virginia State University where she was head of the Art Department. Although not widely known, Meredith is an important figure as a woman working in the field of architecture at a time when both her gender and race put up barriers to her receiving formal training in the field.

SANS is included on the League’s [2020-2021 Seven to Save list](https://www.preservenys.org/blog/seven-to-save-spotlight-sans).

* * *

## Howland Stone Store Museum | Sherwood

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CCV1m1Ape7F/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Howland Stone Store Museum (@howlandstonestoremuseum)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CCV1m1Ape7F/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

The Howland Stone Store Museum, part of the Sherwood Equal Rights Historic District, has deep ties to both the abolitionist and women’s suffrage movements. The Stone Store building has been documented as an authentic Under Ground Railroad site, based on Slocum Howland’s extensive involvement in abolitionist activities. From their website: “In terms of women’s rights, Emily Howland (1927-1929) was honored as a pioneer of the suffrage movement. She was also a major financier of both the New York State Women Suffrage Association and the National American Woman Suffrage Association. Emily Howland, like many women, came to women’s rights through the abolitionist movement, publishing an antislavery letter when she was only seventeen years old; organizing abolitionist activities; and teaching in abolitionist schools.”

Admission is free, and currently by appointment only. [howlandstonestore.org](https://www.howlandstonestore.org/)

The League awarded The Howland Stone Store Museum NYSCA-funded Preserve New York grants in [2006](https://www.preservenys.org/blog/preserve-new-york-grants-2006) (to support State and National Register of Historic Places listings for the hamlet of Sherwood) and [2020](https://www.preservenys.org/blog/preserve-new-york-grants-2020) (to fund a Historic Landscape Report of the 1837 house Opendore).

* * *

## Pollock-Krasner House and Study Center | East Hampton

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/B2ubhRGl0NK/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Christiane Lemieux (@christianelemieux)](https://www.instagram.com/p/B2ubhRGl0NK/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

While Jackson Pollock might be more of a household name, his wife Lee Krasner was an important artist in her own right. The house and studio they shared on the East End of Long Island remains intact, featuring all of the furniture and artifacts that were present when Krasner died in 1984 (Pollock passed away decades earlier, in 1956). She continued creating art in that studio for the rest of her life. Evidence of her expressive painting style can still be seen on the walls, while Pollock left his signature mark on the studio floor. The house, built in 1879 and home to Pollock and Krasner from 1945, is a [National Historic Landmark](https://savingplaces.org/distinctive-destinations/pollock-kranser-house-and-study-center#.YEZoQ51KhPZ).

The museum is open from May-October by advance registration only. [stonybrook.edu/commcms/pkhouse](https://www.stonybrook.edu/commcms/pkhouse/index.php)

* * *

## Women’s Rights National Historical Park | Seneca Falls

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CI5mbNAgLMz/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by WomensRightsNPS (@womensrightsnps)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CI5mbNAgLMz/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

From the National Park Service website: “Women’s Rights National Historical Park tells the story of the first Women’s Rights Convention held in Seneca Falls, NY on July 19-20, 1848. It is a story of struggles for civil rights, human rights, and equality, global struggles that continue today. The efforts of women’s rights leaders, abolitionists, and other 19th century reformers remind us that all people must be accepted as equals.”

The historic homes of the park are currently closed, but you can enjoy an outdoor tour through their Ranger Talks, weather permitting. [nps.gov/wori](https://www.nps.gov/wori/index.htm)

* * *

## Alice Austen House | Staten Island

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CJqq3usBVhZ/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Alice Austen (@aliceaustenhouse)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CJqq3usBVhZ/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

Alice Austen (1866 – 1952) was a prolific photographer, and one of the first women photographers to work outside of the studio, carrying photographic equipment to document life outside. She captured over 7,000 images during her lifetime. Her home on Staten Island was purchased by her grandfather in 1844. It was built in 1690, originally as a one-room Dutch farmhouse, but John Austen spend decades renovating the structure into a Victorian Gothic cottage. Alice Austen moved to the house in the late-1860s and lived there until illness and financial troubles forced her to leave in 1945. For 30 years, Alice Austen lived there with her partner Gertrude Tate. Her photography not only provides a journalistic view of New York, but it also captures intimate relationships between Victorian women through the lens of a lesbian photographer.

The house is open for pre-booked ticketed tours. [aliceausten.org](https://aliceausten.org/)

* * *

## Susan B Anthony Museum & House | Rochester

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CDwttLkhFoy/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Susan B Anthony Museum & House (@susanbhouse)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CDwttLkhFoy/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

From their website: “The National Susan B. Anthony Museum & House in Rochester, New York was the home of the legendary American civil rights leader, and the site of her famous arrest for voting in 1872. This home was the headquarters of the National American Woman Suffrage Association when she was its president. This is also where she died in 1906 at age 86, following her “Failure is Impossible” speech in Baltimore.” The house was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1966.

The museum is open through advance registration only. [susanb.org](https://susanb.org/)

* * *

## The Lucille Ball Desi Arnaz Museum | Jamestown

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CMKwaWXsTrs/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Lucille Ball Desi Arnaz Museum (@lucydesimuseum)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CMKwaWXsTrs/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

Lucille Ball is a Hollywood icon, but she was born in Jamestown, NY. She was a comedic genius and the first woman to run a major television studio. At her museum you can see some of her costumes, props, awards, and recreations of _I Love Lucy_ sets. Lucy’s presence can be felt all around Jamestown. The museum has put together a [Lucytown Driving Tour](https://lucy-desi.com/LucytownTour/), so you can stop by to see her statue at Lucille Ball Memorial Park, visit her grave in Lake View Cemetery, and spot Lucy-themed murals all over the city.

The museum is open, but they recommend advance registration. [lucy-desi.com](https://lucy-desi.com/visit/)

# Celebrating Women's History in New York

Today is International Women’s Day — a great day to spotlight a few sites around New York that celebrate women who made history and helped shape our culture. This is an incomplete list and there are certainly so many more women whose stories went untold. But consider this a starting point if you are looking to do some exploring over the coming weeks and months and want to celebrate women’s history while you do.

* * *

## Shirley Chisholm State Park | Brooklyn

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CDuAm3uggsC/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Shirley Chisholm State Park (@shirleychisholmstatepark)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CDuAm3uggsC/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

Take advantage of a day with good weather and enjoy it outside while celebrating Shirley Chisholm, one of New York’s most iconic women. Chisholm was born in Brooklyn and represented her community in the House of Representatives from 1969-1983. She was the first African American woman elected to Congress, and in 1972, became the first African American candidate for a major party's presidential nomination, and the first woman to run for the Democratic Party's presidential nomination. The park honors her legacy with over 400 acres of land on the Brooklyn waterfront, complete with stunning views of the city and biking and hiking trails.

The park is open every day from 8:00 a.m.-dusk. [parks.ny.gov](https://parks.ny.gov/parks/200/details.aspx)
