Image: NewJerseyAlmanac.com * **[Morven Museum & Garden (Princeton)](http://morven.org/)** Original home built in 1750s by Richard Stockton on 150 acres of land first purchased as 5,500-acre tract in 1701 by his grandfather from William Penn. House remained owned by Stockton family into 20th century, rented in 1930s by Robert Wood Johnson II, chairman of Johnson & Johnson. In 1944, New Jersey Governor Walter Edge purchased Morven from Stockton family, subject to condition that Morven would be given to the state of New Jersey within two years of Edge's death, but transferred ownership to the state during 1954, before he died in 1956. Home became official governor's residence for Governors Meyner, Hughes, Cahill and Byrne from 1955 to January 1982. In 1982, upon inauguration of Governor Kean, Governor's Mansion re-designated to nearby Drumthwacket, a larger mansion, and Morven restored and adapted as a museum under state ownership and operated by nonprofit Morven Foundation. Collections include portraits, landscapes and documents related to history of state and mansion. Gardens include restored kitchen garden with vegetables, herbs and other plantings typical of colonial-era gardens. * * * * **[New Jersey State Museum (Trenton)](http://www.nj.gov/state/museum/index.html)** Established 1895 by legislation, first state museum in country established with education as a primary focus of its mission, original focus on natural history with collection of rocks, minerals and fossils from New Jersey Geological Survey. Located next to New Jersey State Library and State House, operated by state government. Fine Arts collection of over 12,000 works includes paintings, prints, drawings, sculpture and photographs, many of New Jersey scenes or by New Jersey artists. Artists represented include Alfred Stieglitz, Ben Shahn and Jacob Landau. Cultural History collection includes over 13,000 artifacts documenting state's cultural, economic, military, political, and social history. Archaeology and Ethnology collection of over 2 million prehistoric and historic specimens from nearly 100 years of excavation and over 2,000 ethnographic objects. Hi-Def Planetarium with precision projection of over 6,000 stars, largest planetarium in New Jersey. [![Image 8: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/_1360570.jpg?220)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/1360570_orig.jpg)Old Barracks. Image: Library of Congress * **[Old Barracks Museum (Trenton)](http://www.barracks.org/)** Revolutionary War site of George Washington's December 26, 1776, attack on Hessian mercenaries billeted in building following Washington's crossing of Delaware River on previous evening. Washington''s troops captured 30 officers, 918 soldiers and Loyalists, 40 horses, 1,000 muskets and rifles, six cannons and six wagons. Structure originally constructed 1758 during French and Indian War by colony of New Jersey responding to complaints by residents objecting to compulsory quartering of soldiers in their own homes, only surviving one of five such barracks built at that time in New Jersey. During Revolution, at various points barracks used by both British and Americans, with British prisoners of war held in Officers' House and in 1777 as Continental Army hospital. In December 1776, British and Hessian troops occupied Trenton, and briefly stayed in Barracks prior to Battles of Trenton. Old Barracks Museum, located 100 yards from current State House, includes period furniture, kitchenware, weapons and games. Open daily except Sunday year-round, advance reservation for groups of 15 or more.​ * * * * **[National Museum of the American Revolution](http://nationalmuseumoftheamericanrevolution.org/index.htm)****[(Washington Crossing State Park, Titusville)](http://nationalmuseumoftheamericanrevolution.org/index.htm)** Primarily a virtual online museum of history and artifacts from Revolution owned by Swan Historical Foundation with mission to educate people about Revolution. Limited selections from holdings on display at Park include maps, muskets, swords, newspapers and manuscripts, including rare first edition of Thomas Paine's pamphlet entitled _Common Sense_. * **[Roebling Museum (Florence Township)](http://roeblingmuseum.org/)** Site of steel mill and workers' village of Kinkora Works of John A. Roebling and Sons Company, maker of steel and wire used in construction of Brooklyn Bridge, Golden Gate Bridge and other projects. Factory built in 1905, supplemented Trenton plant opened 1848, continued operation under Roebling and subsequent owners past mid-20th century. Roeblings built over 750 houses for workers' families, two workingmen’s hotels and inn, general store, drug store, bakery, auditorium with a library, and recreation hall. Museum in original factory gatehouse, exhibits feature Roebling family, evolution of company, major projects and life of workers. Objects include strand and wire rope, machinery, wooden patterns of machine parts, photographs, paintings and drawings. Roebling Historical Society, which transferred them to the Museum in 2009. * **[Navy Lakehurst Heritage Center (Lakehurst)](http://www.nlhs.com/)**[](http://www.nlhs.com/)**** Operated by nonprofit Navy Lakehurst Historical Society on grounds of Lakehurst Naval Air Station, site of development of Navy airships and famous crash and burning of German Zeppelin Hindenburg on May 6, 1937. Museum includes extensive collection of models of Navy ships and aircraft, uniforms, equipment, also replica of gondola of Hindenburg used in 1975 motion picture "The Hindenburg." Walking tours include site of Hindenburg crash, hangars and other buildings. On-site visits require two-week advance notice for appointments.[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUVDmXvXcbk) * [**National Guard Militia Museum of New Jersey (Sea Girt & Lawrenceville)**](http://www.nj.gov/military/museum/) Operated by New Jersey National Guard with main museum at its Training Center in Sea Girt. Collection includes an outdoor military vehicle and aircraft collection, only Civil War cannon mounted on a carriage on museum display in New Jersey, a Civil War era submarine, and 19th & 20th century small arms collection. Museum also houses extensive manuscript and photograph collection, featuring original and copy material relevant to state political and military history.Holds largest collection of New Jersey related Civil War research material in country, including copies of diaries, letters, newspaper clippings, memoirs, regimental histories and articles. Features rotating exhibits, including current on 70th anniversary of D-Day, and New Jersey National Guard role in liberation of Europe during World War II with chronological history of 102nd Cavalry Group’s progress from the beaches of Normandy to war’s end, as well as experience of New Jerseyans on home front and state's role in manufacturing war materials. Lawrenceville Annex located at Artillery Armory in Lawrenceville with exhibits of weapons, uniforms and other equipment from various periods of service along with about 20 tanks, vehicles and cannon on display outside. * **[Burlington County Prison Museum (Mount Holly)](http://www.prisonmuseum.net/)** Operated from 1811 through 1965 as prison, when closed in 1965 oldest operating prison in US.Designed by Robert Mills, first native-born and trained architect in US with vaulted ceilings of poured concrete and brick and stone construction. Subject of media accounts of paranormal activity, including haunting by male uniformed ghost in basement. Operated as museum by non-profit Prison Museum Association which conducts fundraising, and tours. Designated National Historic Landmark. * **[Corson Poley Center, Burlington County Historical Society (City of Burlington)](http://www.burlingtoncountyhistoricalsociety.org/)** Corson Poley Center contains library and museum, Children’s History Center and three historic houses: Bard-How House, Capt. James Lawrence House and James Fenimore Cooper birthplace. Collection includes art, furniture, quilts and tools, as well as marble mantle from Joseph Bonaparte's estate in Bordentown, chair crafted by William Penn’s son John, rickshaw from Birch carriage company, 19th-century photographs of Revolutionary War veterans, Civil War letters written by a young soldier to his sister, tall case clocks crafted in 18th-century, and door handle of print shop that employed young Benjamin Franklin. * **[African American Heritage Museum of Southern New Jersey (Atlantic City)](http://www.aahmsnj.org/)** Holds over 3,000 objects in collection, including furniture, household items, books, paintings, ceramics and advertising of or related to African Americans, some with stereotypical images or depictions such as Little Black Sambo, Amos & Andy and Buckwheat. Founded 2002 by Ralph E. Hunter, Sr., a retired retail executive with personal collection, relocated to Noyes Arts Garage of Stockton University in Atlantic City in 2013, additional location in Newtonville. Features photos and memorabilia from Atlantic City's Northside African-American neighborhood depicted in _Boardwalk Empire_ book and television series, including original Club Harlem door and sign. [![Image 9: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/5487439_orig.jpg)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/5487439_orig.jpg)USS New Jersey in Camden. Image: Wikimedia Commons by Vladsinger CC BY SA-30 * [**Battleship New Jersey Museum and Memorial (Camden)**](http://www.battleshipnewjersey.org/) Battleship first launched December 1942 from Philadelphia Naval Yard, engaged in major action in World War II, Korean War, Vietnam War and in Middle East until decommissioned for last time in 1991, donated by Navy to non-profit Home Port Alliance in Camden in 1999 and opened as a museum ship in 2001. Self-guided tours, guided group tours, and overnight encampments offered on ship. * * * [![Image 10: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/6248730_orig.jpg)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/6248730_orig.jpg)Indian King Tavern and Museum. Image: Wikimedia Commons/Smallbones CC BY 3.0-SA * [**Indian King Tavern Museum (Haddonfield)**](http://www.indiankingfriends.org/) Colonial tavern and inn built circa 1750 in which New Jersey Provincial Council and General Assembly met from January 29 to March 18, 1777, and later in May and September of that year while British armies occupied towns to north, to officially approve independence, adopt state seal and enact first laws as a state. "Great Room" on tavern's second floor was area's largest non-religious public meeting hall. Continued under private ownership as tavern and inn until 1901, became New Jersey’s first state-owned historic site in 1903, now operated by Department of Environmenmtal Protection. Nonprofit Friends of the Indian King Tavern raises funds for restoration, conducts tours and hosts several open house programs each year with re-enactors, period musicians and speakers. Tavern has period furnishings and housewares, upstairs "Dolley Madison Room" includes bed in which she is claimed to have slept in at a nearby home while a frequent visitor to Haddonfield in 1780s, prior to her marriage to later President James Madison. * * * * [**Paulsdale (Mount Laurel)**](http://www.alicepaul.org/) Childhood family home of women's suffrage leader Alice Paul (1885-1977) maintained by nonprofit Alice Paul Institute. House built circa 1800 on site of then 125-acre farm includes exhibits and also serves as girls leadership development center. Ground floor showcases Paul’s diplomas, family mementos, and suffrage memorabilia, third floor houses Alice Paul Archives and Women’s History Library. Maintains museum, library, and archives collecting and preserving historic documents, photographs and artifacts. Museums collections comprise over 32,000 objects, including costumes, furniture, paintings, prints, ceramics, glass, tools, toys etc. Sponsors exhibitions, publications, and programs. Limited days and hours for on-site visits. * **[T homas Edison National Historical Park (West Orange)](https://www.nps.gov/edis/index.htm)** [![Image 3: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/6157595.jpg?224)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/6157595_orig.jpg)Interior of Edison laboratory. Image: National Park Service Thomas Edison's laboratories and factory buildings on 21-acre site, where after relocating in 1887 from Middlesex County he developed the motion picture camera, improved phonographs, sound recordings, silent and sound movies and nickel-iron alkaline electric storage battery. Museum includes renovated laboratories, factory buildings, artifacts and collection of 60,000 photographs, also reproduction of "Black Maria," first motion picture production studio built by Edison in 1892. Site also includes nearby Edison family home of Glenmont. * * *[![Image 4: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/8531162.jpg?180)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/8531162_orig.jpg) Edison shown in his laboratory in 1901. Image: Library of Congress * **[Afro-American](http://www.cityofjerseycity.org/docs/afroam.shtml)[Historical and Cultural Society Museum (Jersey City)](http://www.cityofjerseycity.org/docs/afroam.shtml)** Located on top floor of Greenville branch of Jersey City Public Library. New Jersey African American history and African artifacts comprise books, newspapers, documents, photographs and memorabilia relating to African American history, including New Jersey slave trade, underground railroad, replica of an urban 1930s kitchen, civil rights movement, NAACP in New Jersey, historic African American churches and genealogical records. * **[Hoboken Historical Museum (Hoboken)](http://www.hobokenmuseum.org/)** Features changing exhibits on history of Hoboken, including prominent citizens such as steamboat and railroad pioneers Stevens family, Frank Sinatra, along with artifacts relating to historic sites, immigration, military roles. Also exhibits art work by local artists. Sponsors education programs for school children; events including house tours, garden tours, film festivals and lectures. Museum publishes many of its own books, including series of oral histories titled "Vanishing Hoboken," as well as extensive digital and online exhibits. * **[Aviation Hall of Fame and Museum of New Jersey (Teterboro)](http://www.njahof.org/)**[](http://www.njahof.org/) Founded in 1972, located at Teterboro Airport. Exhibits on New Jersey aviation and space heritage, displays historic aircraft, helicopters, air and space artifacts, photographs, fine art and extensive model collection. Exhibits include rocket engine that propelled X-15 experimental plane to speed and height records and first American hovercraft. Hall of Fame recognizes prominent aviators, engineers such as Charles Lindbergh, Amelia Earhart, Astronauts Mark and Scott Kelly. Silvio Cavalier Research Library includes over 3,000 volumes. [![Image 5: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/_2069547_orig.jpg)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/2069547_orig.jpg)Liberty Hall. Image: State of New Jersey * **[Liberty Hall Museum at Kean University (Union)](http://www.kean.edu/libertyhall/about/history)** Former home of Livingston and Kean families, members include state's first governor, William Livingston (1776-90), Governor Thomas H. Kean (1982-90) and current Republican Senate Leader Thomas Kean, Jr.. Home originally built on land acquired in 1760 by New York lawyer and colonial legislator William Livingston, member of wealthy Livingston family which owned extensive property along Hudson River north of Manhattan. Livingston built 14-room Georgian mansion country retreat on 120 acres in what was then Elizabethtown and later relocated permanent residence in 1772 from New York to Liberty Hall, subsequently elected as first state governor, died at home in 1790 while serving 14th year as governor. Home remained in family ownership until 1970s transfer to Kean University. Currently operated as museum with holdings including family furniture, paintings, memorabilia, letters of Thomas Jefferson and Benjamin Franklin. Adjacent museum houses New Jersey firehouse memorabilia,including three historic engines, Located on Union campus of Kean University. * * * * **[American Labor Museum-Botto House (Haledon)](http://www.labormuseum.net/)** Botto House National Landmark built 1908 for Italian immigrant and silk mill worker, Pietro Botto and wife Maria. House used in 1913 as central gathering place for labor union organizers of Industrial Workers of the World, who spoke on second-floor balcony to crowds of up to 20,000 silk mill workers striking for eight-hour workday in Paterson Silk Strike. Placed on State and National Register of Historic Sites in 1975 and in 1982 designated as National Landmark. Opened to public as museum In 1983, highlights issues of workers, the workplace, and organized labor with special attention to the ethnicity of working people. Features changing exhibits, restored period rooms and Old World Gardens reflecting early 1900s lifestyle of an immigrant family, free lending library and a Museum Store. Sponsors receptions, lectures, teachers' workshops, student programs and other special events.[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VndQpS_ar4Q) * **[Acorn Hall](http://acornhall.org/)(Morristown[)](http://acornhall.org/)** Headquarters and museum of Morris County Historical Society. Home built for Schermerhorn family in 1853, purchased by Augustus and Mary Crane in 1860 and owned by their descendants in Crane and Hone family until donated in 1971 with contents and surrounding five acres to Historical Society. Exhibits and photographs recognize role of Crane and Hone women in both preservation and women’s suffrage movement. Acorn Hall retains most of its original interior design characteristics and furnishings and serves as authentic representation of early upper-middle class suburban life in Morris County. Society sponsors changing exhibits on local history. * **[Historic Speedwell (Morristown)](http://37.60.235.13/~morrispa/index.php/parks/historic-speedwell)** National Historic Landmark preserves restored eight-acre estate of Stephen Vail, proprietor of Speedwell Ironworks from early to mid-1800s. Morris County Park Commission acquired property in 2002 and opened it to public in 2003. Factory Building, a National Historic Landmark, site of where Stephen Vail's son, Alfred, worked with Samuel F.B. Morse to conduct first successful public demonstration of telegraph on January 11, 1838, making Historic Speedwell ‘Birthplace of the Telegraph.’ Three floors of exhibits profile development of telegraph and to its connections to modern telecommunications. Attached to Factory Building is Wheelhouse with restored 24-foot overshot water wheel. Home includes original furnishings, period antiques, and portraits of Stephen Vail and his first wife Bethiah, painted by Samuel F.B. Morse in 1837 and given to family as gift. [![Image 6: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/332519.jpg)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/332519_orig.jpg)Thomas Nast cartoon. Image: NewJerseyAlmanac.com * [**Macculloch Hall Historical Museum (Morristown)**](http://www.maccullochhall.org/) Museum housed in Federal-style mansion first built in 1810, currently with nine period rooms and three galleries with rotating exhibitions. Holdings include nation’s largest collection of original drawings, watercolors and paintings by political cartoonist Thomas Nast (1840-1902), also a Nast Archives with personal correspondence and photographs, including a family photo album. Other collections of antique furniture, carpets, porcelain and, objects related to the US presidency. Museum’s founder W. Parsons Todd (1877-1976) collected porcelain, 18th and 19th-century American and European furniture, paintings, silver, glass, and American textiles like coverlets and quilts reflecting his personal interests in American history, the presidency, maritime life and Macculloch-Miller family who occupied house from 1810 until Todd's purchase of it in 1949. Decorated rooms open to public display include selections from permanent collection and period furniture and accessories. * * * * **[Museum of Early Trades and Crafts (Madison)](http://www.metc.org/)** Housed in James Library building built 1899-1900 as Madison Public Library named after philanthropist D. (Daniel) Willis James, head of Phelps Dodge & Co. who had become one of wealthiest in US through interests in mining, finance and transportation. Museum founded 1970 by donation from Agnes and Edgar Law Land of their personal collection of pre-industrial hand tools and artifacts. Core collection from Lands later supplemented by gifts from others, now comprises over 8,800 artifacts related to 21 different trades. Collection consists primarily of hand tools and products produced by them, particularly in wood, metal and leather. Interpretive exhibits focused on tools used and trades practiced in New Jersey. * **[USGA Museum (Far Hills)](http://www.usga.org/history/about-museum.html)** Nation’s largest and most significant collection of golf artifacts and documents tracking history of game, particularly in America. Sponsored by United States Golf Association, housed in building designed in 1919 by John Russell Pope, architect who also designed National Archives Building and Jefferson Memorial. After being housed in Manhattan at USGA offices, opened 1972 with relocation of USGA headquarters to Far Hills. Includes Arnold Palmer Center for Golf History with profiles of champions, golf clubs, all 13 USGA national championship trophies and other artifacts. Pynes Putting Course adjacent to building a nine-hole course for visitors to use with replica antique clubs and balls from 19th and early 20th centuries * [**Thomas Edison Center (Edison)**](http://www.menloparkmuseum.org/) Located at site of Thomas Edison's original laboratories in Menlo Park, then a section of Raritan Township, where he worked from 1876 to 1887, when he relocated to much larger complex in West Orange now preserved at Thomas Edison National Historical Park (above). While at Menlo Park, invented phonograph and incandescent electric light, became known as "Wizard of Menlo Park." Property acquired 1933 by state government, but most of original structures destroyed by fire or deterioration, site now in present-day Edison Township and within Edison State Park consists of Art Deco Edison Memorial Tower and small museum and education center. [![Image 7: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/_6991039.jpg)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/6991039_orig.jpg)Morven. Image: NewJerseyAlmanac.com * **[Morven Museum & Garden (Princeton)](http://morven.org/)** Original home built in 1750s by Richard Stockton on 150 acres of land first purchased as 5,500-acre tract in 1701 by his grandfather from William Penn. House remained owned by Stockton family into 20th century, rented in 1930s by Robert Wood Johnson II, chairman of Johnson & Johnson. In 1944, New Jersey Governor Walter Edge purchased Morven from Stockton family, subject to condition that Morven would be given to the state of New Jersey within two years of Edge's death, but transferred ownership to the state during 1954, before he died in 1956. Home became official governor's residence for Governors Meyner, Hughes, Cahill and Byrne from 1955 to January 1982. In 1982, upon inauguration of Governor Kean, Governor's Mansion re-designated to nearby Drumthwacket, a larger mansion, and Morven restored and adapted as a museum under state ownership and operated by nonprofit Morven Foundation. Collections include portraits, landscapes and documents related to history of state and mansion. Gardens include restored kitchen garden with vegetables, herbs and other plantings typical of colonial-era gardens. * * * * **[New Jersey State Museum (Trenton)](http://www.nj.gov/state/museum/index.html)** Established 1895 by legislation, first state museum in country established with education as a primary focus of its mission, original focus on natural history with collection of rocks, minerals and fossils from New Jersey Geological Survey. Located next to New Jersey State Library and State House, operated by state government. Fine Arts collection of over 12,000 works includes paintings, prints, drawings, sculpture and photographs, many of New Jersey scenes or by New Jersey artists. Artists represented include Alfred Stieglitz, Ben Shahn and Jacob Landau. Cultural History collection includes over 13,000 artifacts documenting state's cultural, economic, military, political, and social history. Archaeology and Ethnology collection of over 2 million prehistoric and historic specimens from nearly 100 years of excavation and over 2,000 ethnographic objects. Hi-Def Planetarium with precision projection of over 6,000 stars, largest planetarium in New Jersey. [![Image 8: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/_1360570.jpg?220)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/1360570_orig.jpg)Old Barracks. Image: Library of Congress * **[Old Barracks Museum (Trenton)](http://www.barracks.org/)** Revolutionary War site of George Washington's December 26, 1776, attack on Hessian mercenaries billeted in building following Washington's crossing of Delaware River on previous evening. Washington''s troops captured 30 officers, 918 soldiers and Loyalists, 40 horses, 1,000 muskets and rifles, six cannons and six wagons. Structure originally constructed 1758 during French and Indian War by colony of New Jersey responding to complaints by residents objecting to compulsory quartering of soldiers in their own homes, only surviving one of five such barracks built at that time in New Jersey. During Revolution, at various points barracks used by both British and Americans, with British prisoners of war held in Officers' House and in 1777 as Continental Army hospital. In December 1776, British and Hessian troops occupied Trenton, and briefly stayed in Barracks prior to Battles of Trenton. Old Barracks Museum, located 100 yards from current State House, includes period furniture, kitchenware, weapons and games. Open daily except Sunday year-round, advance reservation for groups of 15 or more.​ * * * * **[National Museum of the American Revolution](http://nationalmuseumoftheamericanrevolution.org/index.htm)****[(Washington Crossing State Park, Titusville)](http://nationalmuseumoftheamericanrevolution.org/index.htm)** Primarily a virtual online museum of history and artifacts from Revolution owned by Swan Historical Foundation with mission to educate people about Revolution. Limited selections from holdings on display at Park include maps, muskets, swords, newspapers and manuscripts, including rare first edition of Thomas Paine's pamphlet entitled _Common Sense_. * **[Roebling Museum (Florence Township)](http://roeblingmuseum.org/)** Site of steel mill and workers' village of Kinkora Works of John A. Roebling and Sons Company, maker of steel and wire used in construction of Brooklyn Bridge, Golden Gate Bridge and other projects. Factory built in 1905, supplemented Trenton plant opened 1848, continued operation under Roebling and subsequent owners past mid-20th century. Roeblings built over 750 houses for workers' families, two workingmen’s hotels and inn, general store, drug store, bakery, auditorium with a library, and recreation hall. Museum in original factory gatehouse, exhibits feature Roebling family, evolution of company, major projects and life of workers. Objects include strand and wire rope, machinery, wooden patterns of machine parts, photographs, paintings and drawings. Roebling Historical Society, which transferred them to the Museum in 2009. * **[Navy Lakehurst Heritage Center (Lakehurst)](http://www.nlhs.com/)**[](http://www.nlhs.com/)**** Operated by nonprofit Navy Lakehurst Historical Society on grounds of Lakehurst Naval Air Station, site of development of Navy airships and famous crash and burning of German Zeppelin Hindenburg on May 6, 1937. Museum includes extensive collection of models of Navy ships and aircraft, uniforms, equipment, also replica of gondola of Hindenburg used in 1975 motion picture "The Hindenburg." Walking tours include site of Hindenburg crash, hangars and other buildings. On-site visits require two-week advance notice for appointments.[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUVDmXvXcbk) * [**National Guard Militia Museum of New Jersey (Sea Girt & Lawrenceville)**](http://www.nj.gov/military/museum/) Operated by New Jersey National Guard with main museum at its Training Center in Sea Girt. Collection includes an outdoor military vehicle and aircraft collection, only Civil War cannon mounted on a carriage on museum display in New Jersey, a Civil War era submarine, and 19th & 20th century small arms collection. Museum also houses extensive manuscript and photograph collection, featuring original and copy material relevant to state political and military history.Holds largest collection of New Jersey related Civil War research material in country, including copies of diaries, letters, newspaper clippings, memoirs, regimental histories and articles. Features rotating exhibits, including current on 70th anniversary of D-Day, and New Jersey National Guard role in liberation of Europe during World War II with chronological history of 102nd Cavalry Group’s progress from the beaches of Normandy to war’s end, as well as experience of New Jerseyans on home front and state's role in manufacturing war materials. Lawrenceville Annex located at Artillery Armory in Lawrenceville with exhibits of weapons, uniforms and other equipment from various periods of service along with about 20 tanks, vehicles and cannon on display outside. * **[Burlington County Prison Museum (Mount Holly)](http://www.prisonmuseum.net/)** Operated from 1811 through 1965 as prison, when closed in 1965 oldest operating prison in US.Designed by Robert Mills, first native-born and trained architect in US with vaulted ceilings of poured concrete and brick and stone construction. Subject of media accounts of paranormal activity, including haunting by male uniformed ghost in basement. Operated as museum by non-profit Prison Museum Association which conducts fundraising, and tours. Designated National Historic Landmark. * **[Corson Poley Center, Burlington County Historical Society (City of Burlington)](http://www.burlingtoncountyhistoricalsociety.org/)** Corson Poley Center contains library and museum, Children’s History Center and three historic houses: Bard-How House, Capt. James Lawrence House and James Fenimore Cooper birthplace. Collection includes art, furniture, quilts and tools, as well as marble mantle from Joseph Bonaparte's estate in Bordentown, chair crafted by William Penn’s son John, rickshaw from Birch carriage company, 19th-century photographs of Revolutionary War veterans, Civil War letters written by a young soldier to his sister, tall case clocks crafted in 18th-century, and door handle of print shop that employed young Benjamin Franklin. * **[African American Heritage Museum of Southern New Jersey (Atlantic City)](http://www.aahmsnj.org/)** Holds over 3,000 objects in collection, including furniture, household items, books, paintings, ceramics and advertising of or related to African Americans, some with stereotypical images or depictions such as Little Black Sambo, Amos & Andy and Buckwheat. Founded 2002 by Ralph E. Hunter, Sr., a retired retail executive with personal collection, relocated to Noyes Arts Garage of Stockton University in Atlantic City in 2013, additional location in Newtonville. Features photos and memorabilia from Atlantic City's Northside African-American neighborhood depicted in _Boardwalk Empire_ book and television series, including original Club Harlem door and sign. [![Image 9: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/5487439_orig.jpg)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/5487439_orig.jpg)USS New Jersey in Camden. Image: Wikimedia Commons by Vladsinger CC BY SA-30 * [**Battleship New Jersey Museum and Memorial (Camden)**](http://www.battleshipnewjersey.org/) Battleship first launched December 1942 from Philadelphia Naval Yard, engaged in major action in World War II, Korean War, Vietnam War and in Middle East until decommissioned for last time in 1991, donated by Navy to non-profit Home Port Alliance in Camden in 1999 and opened as a museum ship in 2001. Self-guided tours, guided group tours, and overnight encampments offered on ship. * * * [![Image 10: Picture](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/6248730_orig.jpg)](https://www.newjerseyalmanac.com/uploads/1/0/9/0/10904396/6248730_orig.jpg)Indian King Tavern and Museum. Image: Wikimedia Commons/Smallbones CC BY 3.0-SA * [**Indian King Tavern Museum (Haddonfield)**](http://www.indiankingfriends.org/) Colonial tavern and inn built circa 1750 in which New Jersey Provincial Council and General Assembly met from January 29 to March 18, 1777, and later in May and September of that year while British armies occupied towns to north, to officially approve independence, adopt state seal and enact first laws as a state. "Great Room" on tavern's second floor was area's largest non-religious public meeting hall. Continued under private ownership as tavern and inn until 1901, became New Jersey’s first state-owned historic site in 1903, now operated by Department of Environmenmtal Protection. Nonprofit Friends of the Indian King Tavern raises funds for restoration, conducts tours and hosts several open house programs each year with re-enactors, period musicians and speakers. Tavern has period furnishings and housewares, upstairs "Dolley Madison Room" includes bed in which she is claimed to have slept in at a nearby home while a frequent visitor to Haddonfield in 1780s, prior to her marriage to later President James Madison. * * * * [**Paulsdale (Mount Laurel)**](http://www.alicepaul.org/) Childhood family home of women's suffrage leader Alice Paul (1885-1977) maintained by nonprofit Alice Paul Institute. House built circa 1800 on site of then 125-acre farm includes exhibits and also serves as girls leadership development center. Ground floor showcases Paul’s diplomas, family mementos, and suffrage memorabilia, third floor houses Alice Paul Archives and Women’s History Library. # Museum Listings and Hours of Operation

1.   Bernhard Museum Complex

[The Berhard Museum Complex](https://www.placer.ca.gov/Facilities/Facility/Details/Bernhard-Museum-77) is open Tuesday-Friday, 1:00-4:00pm, and weekends 11:00am-4:00pm. It is located in Auburn, CA at 291 Auburn-Folsom Road.

Built in 1851 as the Traveler’s Rest Hotel, the Bernhard House has been welcoming visitors for over 150 years. Filled with artifacts and furnishings from a bygone era, the Bernhard House transports visitors to a simpler time. The property also serves as home to the third grade Living History Program.

1.   DeWitt History Museum

[The DeWitt History Museum](https://www.placer.ca.gov/Facilities/Facility/Details/Forest-Hill-Divide-Museum-79) is open on Wednesdays from Noon – 4:00pm. It is located in Auburn, CA at 2985 Richardson Drive.

This museum interprets the World War II-era DeWitt General Army Hospital (1943-1945) and subsequent use of the complex as the DeWitt State Hospital (1946-1972). The museum is the site’s original farm cottage where photographs and historic objects tell the story of the growth and development of the complex and why this former military hospital-turned-psychiatric treatment hospital, is now listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

1.   Foresthill Divide Museum

[](https://www.placer.ca.gov/3385/The-Forest-Hill-Divide-Museum)[The Foresthill Divide Museum](https://www.placer.ca.gov/Facilities/Facility/Details/Forest-Hill-Divide-Museum-79) is open weekends, from 12:00pm – 4:00pm, from Memorial Day through Labor Day weekends. It is located in Foresthill CA, at 24601 Harrison Street.

This museum interprets the history of the town of Foresthill and the surrounding area known as the Foresthill Divide. This gold rush-era community sits at a junction of key transportation routes from Auburn and Yankee Jims and became an important center of trade and travel for the surrounding populations. Displays feature the history of local Native Americans, mining, geology, timber, and 19th-century home life in this mountain community.

1.   Fruitvale Schoolhouse Museum

[The Fruitvale Schoolhouse Museum](https://www.placer.ca.gov/Facilities/Facility/Details/Fruitvale-School-161) is open the second Sunday of each month from 12:00pm-4:00pm. It is located in Lincoln, CA at 3425 Fruitvale Road.

The museum is also available for rentals outside of monthly museum hours. This museum, on Fruitvale Road in Lincoln, is a restored 19th-century schoolhouse. Built in 1888, Fruitvale served local students for 57 years before converting to a community hall. Here, artifacts and images recreate the one-room schoolhouse experience. The Fruitvale School also hosts third grade Living History students and community groups.

1.   Golden Drift Museum

[](https://www.placer.ca.gov/Facilities/Facility/Details/Golden-Drift-Museum-82)[The Golden Drift Museum](https://www.placer.ca.gov/Facilities/Facility/Details/Golden-Drift-Museum-82) is open weekends, from 12:00pm – 4:00pm, from Memorial Day weekend through September. It is located in Dutch Flat, CA at 32820 Main Street.

The museum takes its name from the Golden Drift Historical Society, which in turn was named for a gold mining company that existed in Dutch Flat in the early 1900s. The museum sits on the main street of the Dutch Flat Historic District which is listed on the National Register of Historic places. Here, photographs and objects tell the history of this well-preserved gold rush community and surrounding areas, which was once home to a large and active Chinese community during the 19th century and sits along the route of the transcontinental railroad.

1.   Gold Rush Museum

[](https://www.placer.ca.gov/Facilities/Facility/Details/Gold-Rush-Museum-81)[](https://www.placer.ca.gov/3387/The-Gold-Rush-Museum)[The Gold Rush Museum](https://www.placer.ca.gov/Facilities/Facility/Details/Gold-Rush-Museum-81)is open Thursday through Sunday from 10:30am - 4:00pm. It is located in Auburn, CA at 601 Lincoln Way.

It features a mining tunnel, gold rush twitter wall, many hands-on exhibits and an indoor panning stream that is wheelchair accessible.

1.   Griffith Quarry Museum

[The Griffith Quarry Museum](https://www.placer.ca.gov/Facilities/Facility/Details/Griffith-Quarry-Museum-83) is open weekends, from 12:00pm - 4:00pm. It is located in Penryn, CA at 7504 Rock Springs Road.

This museum is housed in the original Penryn Granite Works office, built by Welsh immigrant Griffith Griffith in 1864. The museum serves as an introduction to the Griffith Quarry Park and illustrates the history of the Penryn-Loomis Basin area, the Griffith family, and importance of the Placer County granite industry which has resulted in this site being listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

1.     

1.   Placer County Museum

[The Placer County Museum](https://www.placer.ca.gov/Facilities/Facility/Details/Placer-County-Museum-84) is open daily from 10:00am – 4:00pm. It is located in Auburn, CA at 101 Maple Street.

This museum is in the historic 1898 Placer County Courthouse, which is a contributor to the Old Auburn Historic District and on the National Register of Historic Places. It presents an overview of Placer County history from the early Nisenan inhabitants through the latter half of the 20th century. It also includes the Placer County Gold collection, the renowned Pate Collection of American Indian artifacts and the original Thomas Kinkade painting "Auburn Centennial".

This museum is in the historic 1898 Placer County Courthouse, which is a contributor to the Old Auburn Historic District and on the National Register of Historic Places. It presents an overview of Placer County history from the early Nisenan inhabitants through the latter half of the 20th century. It also includes the Placer County Gold collection, the renowned Pate Collection of American Indian artifacts and the original Thomas Kinkade painting "Auburn Centennial".

## The .gov means it's official.

Local, state, and federal government websites often end in .gov. Commonwealth of Pennsylvania government websites and email systems use "pennsylvania.gov" or "pa.gov" at the end of the address. Before sharing sensitive or personal information, make sure you're on an official state website.

# Death Records

Learn how to research death records in Pennsylvania and view the available indices for state-issued death certificates.

## Overview

The Commonwealth began to issue death certificates in 1906. Before then, Pennsylvania deaths were only recorded sporadically by the counties and some cities. Information generally found on a death record includes decedent’s name, age, date and place of death, cause of death, occupation, burial place, and parents’ names.

## Death certificate indices (post-1906)

Original death certificates for 1906–1975 are available at the State Archives.You can request an uncertified copy of a death certificate using the [vital records request form](https://www.pa.gov/services/phmc/request-a-birth-or-death-certificate).The 1906-1972 death certificates are accessible online through[Ancestry Pennsylvania](https://www.pa.gov/services/phmc/access-pennsylvania-state-archives-at-ancestry-com)or[Ancestry.com(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/5164/ "View Pennsylvania Death Certificates (post-1906) via Ancestry.com").

Use the following indices to locate the certificate number for a death certificate.

# Death Records

Learn how to research death records in Pennsylvania and view the available indices for state-issued death certificates.

## Overview

The Commonwealth began to issue death certificates in 1906. Before then, Pennsylvania deaths were only recorded sporadically by the counties and some cities. Information generally found on a death record includes decedent’s name, age, date and place of death, cause of death, occupation, burial place, and parents’ names.

## Available death records

Death record availability varies by date range and location.

## Death certificate indices (post-1906)

Original death certificates for 1906–1975 are available at the State Archives.You can request an uncertified copy of a death certificate using the [vital records request form](https://www.pa.gov/services/phmc/request-a-birth-or-death-certificate).The 1906-1972 death certificates are accessible online through[Ancestry Pennsylvania](https://www.pa.gov/services/phmc/access-pennsylvania-state-archives-at-ancestry-com)or[Ancestry.com(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/5164/ "View Pennsylvania Death Certificates (post-1906) via Ancestry.com").

Use the following indices to locate the certificate number for a death certificate.

Within each code number on the index, the names are arranged alphabetically by the first (given) name of the individual.

### Deaths, 1940–1949

The names on the 1940–1949 indices use the Russell Soundex method of indexing. You can use a[Soundex converter(opens in a new tab)](http://searchforancestors.com/utility/soundex.html)to get the surname code number. Within each code number on the index, the names are arranged alphabetically by the first (given) name of the individual.

The DeWitt History Museum is open today, and every Wednesday, from Noon to 4:00 pm. This museum interprets the World War II-era DeWitt General Army Hospital (1943-1945) and subsequent use of the complex as the DeWitt State Hospital (1946-1972). Located at 2985 Richardson Drive in Auburn's DeWitt Government Center, and just like the rest of our museums, Admission is FREE!

The DeWitt History Museum is open today, and every Wednesday, from Noon to 4:00 pm. This museum interprets the World War II-era DeWitt General Army Hospital (1943-1945) and subsequent use of the complex as the DeWitt State Hospital (1946-1972). Located at 2985 Richardson Drive in Auburn's DeWitt Government Center, and just like the rest of our museums, Admission is FREE!

The **Imperial War Museum** (**IWM**), currently branded "**Imperial War Museums**", is a British [national museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_museum "National museum"). Its headquarters are in London, with five branches in England. Founded as the Imperial War Museum in 1917, it was intended to record the civil and military war effort and sacrifice of the United Kingdom and [its Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") during the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"). The museum's remit has since expanded to include all conflicts in which British or Commonwealth forces have been involved since 1914. As of 2012, the museum aims "to provide for, and to encourage, the study and understanding of the history of modern war and 'wartime experience'."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-3)

Originally housed in [the Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace") at [Sydenham Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydenham_Hill "Sydenham Hill"), the museum opened to the public in 1920. In 1924, it moved to space in the [Imperial Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Institute "Imperial Institute") in [South Kensington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Kensington "South Kensington") and in 1936 it acquired a permanent home at the former [Bethlem Royal Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlem_Royal_Hospital "Bethlem Royal Hospital") in [Southwark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwark "Southwark"), which serves as its headquarters. The outbreak of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") saw the museum expand both its collections and its terms of reference, but in the post-war period it entered a period of decline. In 1976 the museum opened [IWM Duxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_Duxford "Imperial War Museum Duxford") at [Duxford airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duxford_Aerodrome "Duxford Aerodrome") in [Cambridgeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridgeshire "Cambridgeshire"), and in 1978 the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") cruiser [HMS _Belfast_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Belfast "HMS Belfast"), which is permanently berthed on the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames") in central London, became a branch of the museum. In 1984, [Churchill War Rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_War_Rooms "Cabinet War Rooms"), an underground wartime command centre in [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster "Westminster"), were opened to the public. In 2002 [IWM North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_North "Imperial War Museum North") opened in [Trafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafford "Trafford"), [Greater Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Manchester "Greater Manchester"), the fifth branch of the museum and the first in the north of England. From the 1980s onwards, the museum's Southwark building underwent a series of multimillion-pound redevelopments, the latest of which was completed in 2022.

The museum's collections include [archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archives "Archives") of personal and official documents, [photographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photographs "Photographs"), [film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film "Film") and [video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video "Video") material, and [oral history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_history "Oral history") recordings, an extensive [library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library "Library"), a large [art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art "Art") collection, and examples of military vehicles and aircraft, equipment, and other artefacts.

The museum is funded by government grants, charitable donations, and revenue generation through commercial activity such as retailing, licensing, and publishing. General admission is free to IWM London (although specific exhibitions require the purchase of a ticket) and IWM North, but an admission fee is levied at the other branches. The museum is an [exempt charity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exempt_charity "Exempt charity") under the Charities Act 1993 and a [non-departmental public body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-departmental_public_body "Non-departmental public body") under the [Department for Culture, Media and Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Culture,_Media_and_Sport "Department for Culture, Media and Sport"). As of April 2024, the chairman of the trustees is [Guy Weston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Weston "Guy Weston"). Since May 2023, Caro Howell has served as the museum's director-general.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-4)

## History of the museum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History of the museum")]

### Establishment: 1917–1921

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Establishment: 1917–1921")]

[![Image 9: Head and shoulders shot of a bald, moustached man looking into the camera.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Alfred_Mond.jpg/250px-Alfred_Mond.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alfred_Mond.jpg)

Sir Alfred Mond, photographed between 1910 and 1920

On 27 February 1917 [Sir Alfred Mond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Mond,_1st_Baron_Melchett "Alfred Mond, 1st Baron Melchett"), a Liberal MP and First Commissioner of Works, wrote to the Prime Minister [David Lloyd George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lloyd_George "David Lloyd George") to propose the establishment of a National War Museum. This proposal was accepted by the [War Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_cabinet#United_Kingdom "War cabinet") on 5 March 1917 and the decision announced in _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_ on 26 March. A committee was established, chaired by Mond, to oversee the collection of material to be exhibited in the new museum.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-6)

This National War Museum Committee set about collecting material to illustrate Britain's war effort by dividing into subcommittees examining such subjects as the Army, the Navy, the production of [munitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munitions "Munitions"), and [women's war work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_roles_in_the_World_Wars "Women's roles in the World Wars").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-7) There was an early appreciation of the need for exhibits to reflect personal experience in order to prevent the collections becoming dead relics. [Sir Martin Conway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Conway,_1st_Baron_Conway_of_Allington "Martin Conway, 1st Baron Conway of Allington"), the museum's first director-general, said that exhibits must "be vitalised by contributions expressive of the action, the experiences, the valour and the endurance of individuals".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-8) The museum's first [curator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curator "Curator") and secretary was [Charles ffoulkes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_ffoulkes "Charles ffoulkes"), who had previously been curator of the [Royal Armouries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Armouries "Royal Armouries") at the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London "Tower of London").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-9) In July 1917 Mond made a visit to the [Western Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Front_(World_War_I) "Western Front (World War I)") in order to study how best to organise the museum's growing collection. While in France he met French government ministers, along with Field Marshal [Sir Douglas Haig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Haig,_1st_Earl_Haig "Douglas Haig, 1st Earl Haig"), [Commander-in-Chief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander-in-chief "Commander-in-chief") (C-in-C) of the [British Expeditionary Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Expeditionary_Force_(World_War_I) "British Expeditionary Force (World War I)") (BEF) on the Western Front, who reportedly took great interest in his work.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-10) In December 1917 the name was changed to the _Imperial_ War Museum after a resolution from the India and Dominions Committee of the museum.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-11)

The museum was opened by King [George V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_V "George V") at [the Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace") on 9 June 1920. During the opening ceremony, Sir Alfred Mond addressed the King on behalf of the committee, saying that "it was hoped to make the museum so complete that every one who took part in the war, however obscurely, would find therein an example or illustration of the sacrifice he or she made" and that the museum "was not a monument of military glory, but a record of toil and sacrifice".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-14) Shortly afterwards the **Imperial War Museum Act 1920** ([10 & 11 Geo. 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10_&_11_Geo._5 "10 & 11 Geo. 5"). c. 16) was passed and established a board of trustees to oversee the governance of the museum. To reflect the museum's Imperial remit the board included appointees of the governments of [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwm1920-15) While the act was being debated, some [parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Parliament of the United Kingdom") felt that the museum would perpetuate an undesirable war spirit and [Lieutenant-Commander Joseph Kenworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Kenworthy,_10th_Baron_Strabolgi "Joseph Kenworthy, 10th Baron Strabolgi") MP said that he would "refuse to vote a penny of public money to commemorate such suicidal madness of civilisation as that which was shown in the late War".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-16) On the [August Bank Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Bank_Holiday "August Bank Holiday") 1920, the first public holiday since the museum's opening, 94,179 visitors were received,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-tpyf-17) and by November 1921, 2,290,719 had visited the museum.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-18)

In 1924 the museum moved to the [Imperial Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Institute "Imperial Institute") building (demolished in the 1950s and 1960s to make way for [Imperial College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_College "Imperial College")) in South Kensington. While this location was more central and in a prestigious area for museums, the accommodation itself proved cramped and inadequate[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-20) and in 1936 a new permanent location was found south of the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames") in Southwark. The building, designed by [James Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lewis_(architect)?action=edit&redlink=1 "James Lewis (architect) (page does not exist)")[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-21) was the former Bethlem Royal Hospital which had been vacated following the hospital's relocation to Beckenham in Kent. The site was owned by [Lord Rothermere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Harmsworth,_1st_Viscount_Rothermere "Harold Harmsworth, 1st Viscount Rothermere"), who had originally intended to demolish the building to provide a public park in what was a severely overcrowded area of London. Eventually the central portion of the hospital building was retained.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-:0-22)

The two extensive wings were removed and the resulting space named [Geraldine Mary Harmsworth Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_Mary_Harmsworth_Park "Geraldine Mary Harmsworth Park"), after Lord Rothermere's mother. Sir Martin Conway described the building as "...a fine building, really quite noble building, with a great portico, a distinguishing dome, and two great wings added to it for the accommodation of lunatics no longer required. This particular building can be made to contain our collection admirably, and we shall preserve from destruction quite a fine building which otherwise will disappear".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-:0-22) The "distinguishing dome" was added by [Sydney Smirke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Smirke "Sydney Smirke") in 1846 and housed the hospital's chapel.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-23) The museum was reopened by the Duke of York (later [King George VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_George_VI "King George VI")) in its new accommodation on 7 July 1936.

### Second World War and after: 1939–1966

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Second World War and after: 1939–1966")]

With the outbreak of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") in 1939, the museum began to collect material documenting the conflict.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-24) In November 1939, during the "[Phoney War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoney_War "Phoney War")", the museum appeared in the opening sequence of the [GPO Film Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPO_Film_Unit "GPO Film Unit") production _The First Days_, in which children are seen playing on some of the museum's German artillery pieces captured during the First World War.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-25) With the [Dunkirk evacuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkirk_evacuation "Dunkirk evacuation") in May–June 1940, the British Army's shortage of equipment saw eighteen of the museum's artillery pieces return to military service.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-charman103-26) The museum's trench clubs were used by the [Home Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Guard_(United_Kingdom) "Home Guard (United Kingdom)"), while other items such as sights and optical instruments were returned to the Ministry of Supply. The museum refused to return some historic items such as a naval gun from [HMS _Lance_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Lance_(1914) "HMS Lance (1914)") (which had fired Britain's first shot of the First World War) or a gun served by [Victoria Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Cross "Victoria Cross")-winning boy seaman [Jack Cornwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Cornwell "Jack Cornwell").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-charman103-26) The museum was closed for the duration of the war in September 1940 with the onset of [the Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blitz "The Blitz"). On 31 January 1941 the museum was struck by a _[Luftwaffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luftwaffe "Luftwaffe")_ bomb which fell on the naval gallery. A number of ship models were damaged by the blast and a [Short Type 184](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_Type_184 "Short Type 184") seaplane, which had flown at the [Battle of Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Jutland "Battle of Jutland"), was destroyed.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-IWMLguide2-27) While closed to the public the museum's building was used for a variety of purposes connected to the war effort, such as a repair garage for government motor vehicles, a centre for Air Raid Precautions civil defence lectures and a fire fighting training school.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-28)

In October 1945 the museum mounted a temporary exhibition, the first since the end of the war in August, which showcased technologies developed by the [Petroleum Warfare Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_Warfare_Department "Petroleum Warfare Department"). These included the submarine fuel pipeline [PLUTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Pluto "Operation Pluto"), the fog dispersal method [FIDO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog_Investigation_and_Dispersal_Operation "Fog Investigation and Dispersal Operation"), and flame weapons such as the [Churchill Crocodile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Churchill_Crocodile "Churchill Crocodile") and Wasp [Universal Carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Carrier "Universal Carrier").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-29) Due to bomb damage to the building and exhibits, the museum was obliged to reopen its galleries piecemeal and opened a portion of its galleries in November 1946.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-IWMLguide2-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Imperial_War_Museum_page_7-30) A third of the galleries were opened in 1948 and a further wing opened in 1949.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-31)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-32) In 1953, with Commonwealth forces engaged in [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War") and [Malaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayan_Emergency "Malayan Emergency") the museum began its current policy of collecting material from all modern conflicts in which British or Commonwealth forces were involved.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-IWMLguide2-27) Despite this expansion of remit, the early postwar period was a period of decline for the museum. [Noble Frankland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_Frankland "Noble Frankland"), the museum's director from 1960 to 1982, described the museum's galleries in 1955 as appearing "dingy and neglected [and in a] dismal state of decay" the museum's "numerous stunning exhibits" notwithstanding.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-33)

### Redevelopment and expansion: 1966–2012

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Redevelopment and expansion: 1966–2012")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/15inchgunsatImperialWarMuseumLondon.jpg/250px-15inchgunsatImperialWarMuseumLondon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:15inchgunsatImperialWarMuseumLondon.jpg)

15-inch guns outside the museum; the nearer gun from [HMS _Ramillies_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Ramillies_(07) "HMS Ramillies (07)"), the other from [HMS _Resolution_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Resolution_(09) "HMS Resolution (09)")

In 1966 the museum's Southwark building was extended to provide collections storage and other facilities, the first major expansion since the museum had moved to the site. The development also included a purpose-built cinema.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-34) In 1967 the museum acquired a pair of [15-inch naval guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BL_15-inch_Mk_I_naval_gun "BL 15-inch Mk I naval gun"). One had been mounted on the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy")'s [HMS _Ramillies_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Ramillies_(07) "HMS Ramillies (07)") and the other on both [HMS _Resolution_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Resolution_(09) "HMS Resolution (09)") and [HMS _Roberts_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Roberts_(F40) "HMS Roberts (F40)"). Both had been fired in action during the Second World War. They went on permanent display outside the museum in May 1968.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-35) The acquisition of these guns, representative of the [dreadnought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreadnought "Dreadnought") era of British [battleships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship "Battleship"), led the museum to seek to acquire a [6-inch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BL_6-inch_Mk_XXIII_naval_gun "BL 6-inch Mk XXIII naval gun") triple turret that would be representative of a number of classes of British [cruisers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruiser "Cruiser").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Wingate101-36) This would eventually lead to the preservation of the Royal Navy [light cruiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_cruiser "Light cruiser")[HMS _Belfast_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Belfast "HMS Belfast"), which became a branch of the museum in 1978.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-37) Later in 1968 on 13 October the museum was attacked by an [arsonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsonist "Arsonist"), Timothy John Daly, who claimed he was acting in protest against the exhibition of [militarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Militarism "Militarism") to children. He caused damage valued at approximately £200,000, not counting the loss of irreplaceable books and documents. On his conviction in 1969 he was sentenced to four years in prison.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-38)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-39)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/V-1_flying_bomb_on_display_at_Imperial_War_Museum.jpg/250px-V-1_flying_bomb_on_display_at_Imperial_War_Museum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:V-1_flying_bomb_on_display_at_Imperial_War_Museum.jpg)

[V-1 flying bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V-1_flying_bomb "V-1 flying bomb") on display

In 1969 RAF Duxford, a [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") fighter airfield in [Cambridgeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridgeshire "Cambridgeshire") was declared surplus to requirements by the [Ministry of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_(United_Kingdom) "Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)"). Needing further space, the museum duly requested permission to use part of the site as temporary storage. The entire site was later transferred to the museum in February 1976 and Duxford, now referred to as [Imperial War Museum Duxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_Duxford "Imperial War Museum Duxford") became the museum's first branch.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Frankland-40) Also during the 1970s the government raised the possibility of the museum taking over the historic [Cabinet War Rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_War_Rooms "Cabinet War Rooms") in [Whitehall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehall "Whitehall"). The museum was reluctant due to its new commitments related to Duxford and HMS _Belfast_, but agreed in 1982.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Holmes-41)

By 1983 the museum was again looking to redevelop the Southwark site and approached engineering firm [Arup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arup_Group "Arup Group") to plan a phased programme of works that would expand the building's exhibition space, provide appropriate environmental controls to protect collections, and improve facilities for visitors. The following year, in April 1984, the Cabinet War Rooms were opened to the public as a branch of the museum.

The first phase of the works to the Southwark building started in 1986 and were completed in 1989, during which time the museum was closed to the public. The work included the conversion of what was previously the hospital's courtyard into a centrepiece Large Exhibits Gallery. This gallery featured a strengthened ground floor (to support the weight of very heavy exhibits), a first floor [mezzanine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mezzanine_(architecture) "Mezzanine (architecture)") and second storey viewing balcony. Into this space were placed tanks, artillery pieces, vehicles, ordnance and aircraft from the First World War to the [Falklands War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falklands_War "Falklands War").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-arupjournal-42) For some years the museum was marketed as "The _new_ Imperial War Museum".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-43) This atrium, with its concentration of military hardware, has been described as "the biggest boys' bedroom in London".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-44) This first phase cost £16.7 million (of which £12 million was provided by the government) and the museum was reopened by [The Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") on 29 June 1989.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-45) In 1990, the museum was awarded National Heritage [Museum of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_the_Year "Museum of the Year").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-46)

Suspended aircraft include a [Sopwith Camel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sopwith_Camel "Sopwith Camel"), [Heinkel He 162](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinkel_He_162 "Heinkel He 162") and (partially obscured) [Supermarine Spitfire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermarine_Spitfire "Supermarine Spitfire") number R/6915, which flew in the [Battle of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain "Battle of Britain") and shot down three aircraft.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-warbird-47)

In September 1992 the museum was the target of a [Provisional Irish Republican Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army "Provisional Irish Republican Army") attack against London tourist attractions. Two [incendiary devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incendiary_device "Incendiary device") were found in a basement gallery, but were extinguished by staff before the arrival of the [fire brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Fire_Brigade "London Fire Brigade"), and caused only minor damage.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-48)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-49)

The second stage of the redevelopment of the Southwark building, during which the museum remained open to the public, was completed in 1994.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-arupjournal-42) During the 1990s, while these works were going on, the museum was also seeking to open a branch in the north of England. 71 sites were offered for consideration by 36 local councils and in January 1999 the then [Culture Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Digital,_Culture,_Media_and_Sport "Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport")[Chris Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Smith,_Baron_Smith_of_Finsbury "Chris Smith, Baron Smith of Finsbury") formally launched a project to construct a new branch of the museum, [Imperial War Museum North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_North "Imperial War Museum North"), in [Trafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafford "Trafford"), [Greater Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Manchester "Greater Manchester").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Glancey-50) 1999 also saw the Museum's first Poetry Residency, launching the long-lasting "Search and Create" initiative in which war-themed poems were installed among the artefacts to stimulate public and schools engagement.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-PoetryHunt-51)

The following year, 2000, the final phase of the Southwark redevelopment was completed. The development included the installation of the museum's _Holocaust Exhibition_ which was opened by the Queen on 6 June 2000. This was the first permanent exhibition dedicated to the [Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust "Holocaust") in a UK museum; its development had taken five years at a cost of £5 million.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-52) Two years later, in July 2002, Imperial War Museum North was opened.

Between 2004 and 2010 the museum was a partner in a national learning project entitled "Their Past Your Future" (TPYF), part of the [Big Lottery Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Lottery_Fund "Big Lottery Fund")'s Veterans Reunited programme to commemorate the 60th anniversary of the end of the Second World War.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-VeteransEval-53) A partnership between the IWM, the [Museums, Libraries and Archives Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museums,_Libraries_and_Archives_Council "Museums, Libraries and Archives Council"), and Scottish, Northern Irish and Welsh museum authorities, phase one included a touring exhibition seen by more than two million people,[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-54) overseas educational visits[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-55) and further activities run by local authorities. A second phase took a wider 20th-century historical remit; it comprised a learning programme using overseas visits and [social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media "Social media"), and a professional development scheme for educators.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-56) A digital archive of the project,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-57) online exhibitions and learning resources were also produced.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-58)

In October 2011 the museum [rebranded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand "Brand") itself as Imperial War Museums, the initials IWM forming the basis of a new corporate logo.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-59)

In September 2011 the museum secured funding from [NESTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NESTA "NESTA"), the [Arts and Humanities Research Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_and_Humanities_Research_Council "Arts and Humanities Research Council") and [Arts Council England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_Council_England "Arts Council England") to develop "social interpretation" systems to allow visitors to comment on, collect, and share museum objects via social media.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-NESTA-60) These systems were incorporated in "A Family in Wartime", an exhibition at IWM London depicting British family life during the Second World War, which opened in April 2012.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-socintguardian-61)

Duke of Cambridge") became the foundation's patron.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-64) In a speech at IWM London on 11 October 2012, Prime Minister [David
