## Branches

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Branches")]

From the 1970s onwards the Imperial War Museum began to expand onto other sites. The first branch, [Imperial War Museum Duxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_Duxford "Imperial War Museum Duxford") opened to the public on a regular basis in June 1976.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-73)[HMS _Belfast_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Belfast "HMS Belfast") became a branch of the museum in 1978.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Wingate-74) The [Churchill War Rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_War_Rooms "Cabinet War Rooms") opened in 1984,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-75) and [Imperial War Museum North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_North "Imperial War Museum North") in 2002.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-76)

### Imperial War Museum London

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Imperial War Museum London")]

#### Architecture and layout

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Architecture and layout")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/BethlemSteelEngraving1828_%28no_caption%29.png/250px-BethlemSteelEngraving1828_%28no_caption%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BethlemSteelEngraving1828_(no_caption).png)

A view of [Bethlem Royal Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlem_Royal_Hospital "Bethlem Royal Hospital") in 1828

The museum has occupied the former Bethlem Royal Hospital on [Lambeth Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeth_Road "Lambeth Road") since 1936. The hospital building was designed by the hospital surveyor, James Lewis, from plans submitted by [John Gandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Peter_Gandy "John Peter Gandy") and other architects, and construction completed in October 1814. The hospital consisted of a range of buildings 580 feet long with a basement and three storeys, parallel to [Lambeth Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeth_Road "Lambeth Road"), with a central entrance under a [portico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portico "Portico").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-britishhistoryonline-77)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Imperial_War_Museum_1.jpg/250px-Imperial_War_Museum_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Imperial_War_Museum_1.jpg)

15-inch guns and copper dome

The building was substantially altered in 1835 by architect [Sydney Smirke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Smirke "Sydney Smirke"). In order to provide more space, he added blocks at either end of the frontage, and galleried wings on either side of the central portion. He also added a small single-storey lodge, still in existence, at the [Lambeth Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeth_Road "Lambeth Road") gate. Later, between 1844 and 1846, the central [cupola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupola "Cupola") was replaced with a copper-clad dome in order to expand the [chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel "Chapel") beneath. The building also featured a theatre in a building to the rear of the site.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-britishhistoryonline-77)

The building remained substantially unchanged until vacated by the hospital in 1930. After the [freehold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freehold_(English_law) "Freehold (English law)") was purchased by [Lord Rothermere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Rothermere "Lord Rothermere"), the wings were demolished to leave the original central portion (with the dome now appearing disproportionately tall) and Smirke's later wings. When the museum moved into the building in 1936 the ground floor of the central portion was occupied by the principal art gallery, with the east wing housing the Naval gallery and the west wing the Army gallery. The Air Force gallery was housed in the former theatre. The first floor comprised further art galleries (including rooms dedicated to [Sir William Orpen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_William_Orpen "Sir William Orpen") and [Sir John Lavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_John_Lavery "Sir John Lavery")), a gallery on [women's war work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_roles_in_the_World_Wars "Women's roles in the World Wars"), and exhibits relating to transport and signals. The first floor also housed the museum's photograph collection. The second floor housed the museum's library in its west wing, and in the east wing the [map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Map "Map") collection and stored pictures and drawings.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-78) This division of exhibits by service, and by civil or military activity, persisted until a wide-ranging redisplay of the galleries from the 1960s onwards. In September 1972 the building received Grade II [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") status.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-79)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Supermarine_Spitfire_at_Imperial_War_Museum_London.jpg/250px-Supermarine_Spitfire_at_Imperial_War_Museum_London.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Supermarine_Spitfire_at_Imperial_War_Museum_London.jpg)

Top view of the Supermarine Spitfire

The original hospital building is now largely occupied by corporate offices. The 1966 extension houses the library, art store, and document archives while the 1980s redevelopments created exhibition space over five floors. The first stage created 8,000 m 2 of gallery space of which 4,600 m 2 was new, and the second provided a further 1,600 m 2.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-arupjournal-42) The final phase, the Southwest Infill, was partly funded by a £12.6 million grant from the [Heritage Lottery Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_Lottery_Fund "Heritage Lottery Fund")[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-80) and provided 5,860m 2 of gallery space and educational facilities over six floors.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-81) Before the 2013–14 redevelopment, the basement was occupied by permanent galleries on the First and Second World Wars, and of conflicts after 1945. The ground floor comprised the atrium, cinema, temporary exhibition spaces, and visitor facilities. The first floor included the atrium mezzanine, education facilities, and a permanent gallery, _Secret War_, exploring [special forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_forces "Special forces"), [espionage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espionage "Espionage") and [covert operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covert_operation "Covert operation"). The second floor included the atrium viewing balcony, two art galleries, a temporary exhibition area and the permanent _Crimes against Humanity_ exhibition. The third floor housed the permanent _Holocaust Exhibition_, and the fourth floor, a [vaulted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vault_(architecture) "Vault (architecture)") roof space, accommodated the Lord Ashcroft Gallery. Opened in November 2010 the gallery exhibits the museum's [Victoria Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Cross "Victoria Cross") (VC) and [George Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cross "George Cross") collection, alongside the private VC collection amassed by [Michael Ashcroft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ashcroft,_Baron_Ashcroft "Michael Ashcroft, Baron Ashcroft"), 241 medals in total.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-arupjournal-42)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-82)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-83) The Lord Ashcroft Collection was on loan for ten years,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-84) was extended for a further five years because of COVID, and the termination of the loan was first confirmed in July 2024, resulting in the closure on 1 June 2025.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-85)

In August 2019, the museum announced plans to spend over £30 million on a new set of galleries over two floors at its London site covering the Holocaust and its importance in World War II.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-86) The galleries opened in October 2021 to replace the existing permanent exhibition.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-87)

#### All Saints Annexe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: All Saints Annexe")]

In 1989 the museum acquired the All Saints Annexe, a former hospital building in Austral Street off [West Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Square "West Square"). The 1867 building, which backs onto [Geraldine Mary Harmsworth Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_Mary_Harmsworth_Park "Geraldine Mary Harmsworth Park"), was originally an orphanage opened by local [philanthropist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philanthropist "Philanthropist")[Charlotte Sharman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Sharman "Charlotte Sharman"), then later used as a hospital. It housed the museum's photographic, film and sound archives, and offices.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-88)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-89)

### Imperial War Museum Duxford

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Imperial War Museum Duxford")]

Main article: [Imperial War Museum Duxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_Duxford "Imperial War Museum Duxford")

[![Image 20: Various aircraft, large and small, exhibited in a hangar.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Imperialwarmuseumduxfordairspacecrop.jpg/250px-Imperialwarmuseumduxfordairspacecrop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Imperialwarmuseumduxfordairspacecrop.jpg)

AirSpace at [IWM Duxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_Duxford "Imperial War Museum Duxford")

Imperial War Museum Duxford, near the village of [Duxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duxford "Duxford") in [Cambridgeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridgeshire "Cambridgeshire"), is Britain's largest [aviation museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation_museum "Aviation museum").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Holt-90) Duxford houses the museum's large exhibits, including nearly 200 [aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft "Aircraft"), military vehicles, artillery and minor naval vessels in seven main exhibitions buildings.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-A&V-91) The site also provides storage space for the museum's collections of film, photographs, documents, books and artefacts. The site accommodates a number of [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army") regimental museums, including those of the [Parachute Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachute_Regiment_(United_Kingdom) "Parachute Regiment (United Kingdom)") and the [Royal Anglian Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Anglian_Regiment "Royal Anglian Regiment").

Based on the historic [Duxford Aerodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duxford_Aerodrome "Duxford Aerodrome"), the site was originally operated by the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") (RAF) during the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"). During the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") Duxford played a prominent role during the [Battle of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain "Battle of Britain") and was later used by [United States Army Air Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Air_Forces "United States Army Air Forces") fighter units in support of the [daylight bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_bombing_during_World_War_II#US_bombing_in_Europe "Strategic bombing during World War II") of Germany. Duxford remained an active RAF airfield until 1961. Many of Duxford's original buildings, such as [hangars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangar "Hangar") used during the Battle of Britain, are still in use. A number of these buildings are of architectural or historic significance and over thirty have [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") status.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-IWMDhistoric-92) The site also features a number of purpose-built exhibition buildings, such as the [Stirling Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling_Prize "Stirling Prize")-winning American Air Museum, designed by [Sir Norman Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Foster_(architect) "Norman Foster (architect)"). The site remains an active airfield and is used by a number of civilian flying companies, and hosts regular [air shows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_show "Air show"). The site is operated in partnership with [Cambridgeshire County Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridgeshire_County_Council "Cambridgeshire County Council") and the Duxford Aviation Society, a charity formed in 1975 to preserve [civil aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_aircraft "Civil aircraft") and promote appreciation of British civil aviation history.

### HMS _Belfast_ (1938)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: HMS Belfast (1938)")]

Main article: [HMS Belfast (C35)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Belfast_(C35) "HMS Belfast (C35)")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/HMS_Belfast_3.jpg/250px-HMS_Belfast_3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HMS_Belfast_3.jpg)

HMS _Belfast_ at her berth in the [Pool of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_of_London "Pool of London")

HMS _Belfast_, a [Town class cruiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_class_cruiser_(1936) "Town class cruiser (1936)"), was launched in 1938 and served throughout the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), participating in the December 1943 [Battle of North Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_North_Cape "Battle of North Cape") and firing some of the first shots of [Operation Overlord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Overlord "Operation Overlord"), the Allied invasion of Normandy in June 1944. She saw further combat in the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War"). Expected to be disposed of as scrap after she was decommissioned in 1963, in 1967 efforts were initiated to preserve _Belfast_ as a museum ship. A joint committee of the Imperial War Museum, the [National Maritime Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Maritime_Museum "National Maritime Museum") and the [Ministry of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_(UK) "Ministry of Defence (UK)") was established, and reported in June 1968 that preservation was practical. In 1971 the government decided against preservation, prompting the formation of the private HMS _Belfast_ Trust to campaign for her to be saved for the nation. The Trust was successful in its efforts, and the government transferred the ship to the Trust in July 1971. Brought to London, she was moored on the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames") near [Tower Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Bridge "Tower Bridge") in the [Pool of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_of_London "Pool of London"). Opened to the public in October 1971 _Belfast_ became a branch of the Imperial War Museum on 1 March 1978, being acknowledged by the then [Secretary of State for Education and Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Education_and_Science "Secretary of State for Education and Science"), [Shirley Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Williams "Shirley Williams"), as "a unique demonstration of an important phase of our history and technology".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-93) In service for 24 years HMS _Belfast_ was in Frankland's opinion, capable of representing "a whole generation of [historical evidence]".[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-94)

In 2017, the name of the exhibit was changed to "HMS _Belfast_ 1938" to reflect that one of the Royal Navy's new [Type 26 frigates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_26_frigate "Type 26 frigate") had been given the name HMS _Belfast_.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-95)

### Churchill War Rooms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Churchill War Rooms")]

Main article: [Churchill War Rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Churchill_War_Rooms "Churchill War Rooms")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/MapRoomCabinetWarRoomsTrim.jpg/250px-MapRoomCabinetWarRoomsTrim.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MapRoomCabinetWarRoomsTrim.jpg)

The Map Room of the [Cabinet War Rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Churchill_Museum_and_Cabinet_War_Rooms "Churchill Museum and Cabinet War Rooms")

The Cabinet War Rooms is an underground complex that served as a British government command centre throughout the Second World War. Located beneath the [Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HM_Treasury "HM Treasury") building in the [Whitehall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehall "Whitehall") area of [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster "Westminster"), the facilities became operational in 1939 and were in constant use until their abandonment in August 1945 after the [surrender of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrender_of_Japan "Surrender of Japan"). Their historical value was recognised early on, and the public were able to visit by appointment. However, the practicalities of allowing public access to a site beneath a working government office meant that only 4,500 of 30–40,000 annual applicants to visit the War Rooms could be admitted.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Holmes-41) The museum agreed to take over the administration of the site in 1982,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Holmes-41) a development keenly supported by the then Prime Minister [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher"), an admirer of Britain's wartime Prime Minister [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill"). Thatcher opened the War Rooms in April 1984. In 2003 a further suite of rooms, used as accommodation by Churchill, his wife and close associates, were added to the museum. The restoration of these rooms, which since the war had been stripped out and used for storage, cost £7.5 million.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-96) In 2005 the War Rooms were rebranded as the Churchill Museum and Cabinet War Rooms, with 850 m 2 of the site redeveloped as a biographical museum exploring Churchill's life. The development of the Churchill Museum cost a further £6 million. The centrepiece is a 15 m interactive table which enables visitors to access digitised material, particularly from the [Churchill Archives Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Churchill_Archives_Centre "Churchill Archives Centre"), via an "electronic filing cabinet".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-97) The museum was renamed the Churchill War Rooms in 2010.

### Imperial War Museum North

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Imperial War Museum North")]

Main article: [Imperial War Museum North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_North "Imperial War Museum North")

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/ImperialWarMuseumNorth02Trim.jpg/250px-ImperialWarMuseumNorth02Trim.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ImperialWarMuseumNorth02Trim.jpg)

Entrance of [Imperial War Museum North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_North "Imperial War Museum North") in [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester")

The Imperial War Museum North was opened in [Trafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafford "Trafford"), [Greater Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Manchester "Greater Manchester"), in 2002. It was the first branch of the museum outside southeast England, and the first to be purpose-built as a museum. Designed by architect [Daniel Libeskind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Libeskind "Daniel Libeskind"), with Manchester-based architects Leach Rhodes Walker providing implementation services,[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-98) The Imperial War Museum North was Libeskind's first building in Britain. Libeskind's building, overlooking the [Manchester Ship Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Ship_Canal "Manchester Ship Canal") at [Salford Quays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salford_Quays "Salford Quays"), was based on the concept of a globe shattered by conflict into shards and reassembled. These shards, representing earth, air and water, give the building its shape.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-99) Originally budgeted at £40 million, the museum was completed for £28.5 million after anticipated funding was not forthcoming. The museum was funded by local, national and European development agencies, by private donations and by [Peel Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peel_Holdings "Peel Holdings"), a local transport and property company which contributed £12.5 million.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-100)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-101)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Russian_T38_-_85_%286264920102%29.jpg/250px-Russian_T38_-_85_%286264920102%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Russian_T38_-_85_(6264920102).jpg)

[T-34-85](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-34-85 "T-34-85") tank on display

The museum's first floor main gallery space houses the permanent exhibitions. These consist of a chronological display which runs around the gallery's 200m perimeter and six thematic displays in "silos" within the space. The walls of the gallery space are used as screens for the projection of an hourly audiovisual presentation, the Big Picture. The main gallery, described as cavernous and dramatic,[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Herbert2-102)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-103) includes objects such as a Russian [T-34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-34 "T-34") tank, a [United States Marine Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps "United States Marine Corps")[AV-8A Harrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AV-8A_Harrier "AV-8A Harrier") jet, and a British [13-pounder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_QF_13_pounder "Ordnance QF 13 pounder") field gun which fired the [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army")'s first shot of the First World War.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-104) The museum also hosts a programme of temporary exhibitions, mounted in a separate gallery.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-105)

## Collections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Collections")]

See also: [Category:Collection of the Imperial War Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Collection_of_the_Imperial_War_Museum "Category:Collection of the Imperial War Museum")

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Lieutenant_General_Bernard_Montgomery%2C_commanding_the_British_Eighth_Army_in_North_Africa%2C_in_the_turret_of_his_Grant_command_tank_at_El_Alamein%2C_5_November_1942._E18980.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lieutenant_General_Bernard_Montgomery,_commanding_the_British_Eighth_Army_in_North_Africa,_in_the_turret_of_his_Grant_command_tank_at_El_Alamein,_5_November_1942._E18980.jpg)

The museum's collection includes this photograph of [Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Montgomery "Bernard Montgomery") in his tank along with the tank, his command caravans, staff car[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-106) and his papers.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-107)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-montgomerydocs-108)

The Imperial War Museum's original collections date back to the material amassed by the National War Museum Committee. The present departmental organisation came into being during the 1960s as part of Frankland's reorganisation of the museum. The 1970s saw [oral history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_history "Oral history") gain increasing prominence and in 1972 the museum created the Department of Sound Records (now the Sound Archive) to record interviews with individuals who had experienced the First World War. The museum maintains an [online database of its collections](http://www.iwm.org.uk/collections/search).[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-109)

### Documents

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Documents")]

The museum's documents archive seeks to collect and preserve the private papers of individuals who have experienced modern warfare. The archive's holdings range from the papers of senior British and Commonwealth army, navy and air officers, to the letters, diaries and memoirs of lower-ranked servicemen and of civilians. The collection includes the papers of Field Marshals [Bernard Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Montgomery "Bernard Montgomery"),[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-montgomerydocs-108) and [John French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_French,_1st_Earl_of_Ypres "John French, 1st Earl of Ypres").[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-110) The archive also includes large collections of foreign documents, such as captured German Second World War documents previously held by the Cabinet Office Historical Section, Air Historical Branch and other British government bodies. The foreign collection also includes captured Japanese material transferred from the Cabinet Office. The collection also includes files on Victoria and George Cross recipients, and correspondence relating to the BBC documentary _The Great War_.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-111) The documents collection also includes the [UK National Inventory of War Memorials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_National_Inventory_of_War_Memorials "UK National Inventory of War Memorials").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwmdocs-112) In 2012 the museum reported its documents collection to contain 24,800 collections of papers.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwm2012p62-113)

### Art

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Art")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/The_Nuremberg_Trial%2C_1946_%281946%29_%28Art._IWM_ART_LD_5798%29.jpg/250px-The_Nuremberg_Trial%2C_1946_%281946%29_%28Art._IWM_ART_LD_5798%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Nuremberg_Trial,_1946_(1946)_(Art._IWM_ART_LD_5798).jpg)

_[The Nuremberg Trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Nuremberg\_Trial "The Nuremberg Trial")_, 1946, by [Laura Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Knight "Laura Knight")

The museum's art collection includes paintings, prints, drawings, sculpture, and works in film, photography and [sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_art "Sound art").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwmart-114) The collection originated during the First World War, when the museum acquired works that it had itself commissioned, as well as works commissioned by the Ministry of Information's [British War Memorials Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_War_Memorials_Committee "British War Memorials Committee"). As early as 1920 the art collection held over 3,000 works[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-115) and included pieces by [John Singer Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Singer_Sargent "John Singer Sargent"), [Wyndham Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis "Wyndham Lewis"), [John Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Nash_(artist) "John Nash (artist)") and [Christopher Nevinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Nevinson "Christopher Nevinson"). Notable First World War works include Sargent's _[Gassed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gassed\_(painting) "Gassed (painting)")_[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-116) and other works commissioned for an unbuilt [Hall of Remembrance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall_of_Remembrance "Hall of Remembrance").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-IWMHoR-117) The collection expanded again after the Second World War, receiving thousands of works sponsored by the Ministry of Information's [War Artists' Advisory Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Artists'_Advisory_Committee "War Artists' Advisory Committee").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-118)

In 1972 the museum established the Artistic Records Committee (since renamed the Art Commissions Committee) to commission artists to cover contemporary conflicts.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-119) Commissioned artists include [Ken Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Howard_(artist) "Ken Howard (artist)"), [Linda Kitson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Kitson "Linda Kitson"), [John Keane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Keane_(artist) "John Keane (artist)"), [Peter Howson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Howson "Peter Howson"), [Steve McQueen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_McQueen_(director) "Steve McQueen (director)") (see [_Queen and Country_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_and_Country_(artwork) "Queen and Country (artwork)")) and [Langlands & Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_&_Bell "Langlands & Bell"), responding to conflicts in Northern Ireland, the Falklands, the Persian Gulf, Bosnia, Iraq and Afghanistan.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-120)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-121)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-122)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-123)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-124) The collection also includes over twenty thousand items of publicity material such as posters, postcards, and proclamations from both world wars, and more recent material such as posters issued by anti-war organisations such as the [Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_for_Nuclear_Disarmament "Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament") and the [Stop the War Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop_the_War_Coalition "Stop the War Coalition").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwmart-114) The museum's collection is represented in digital resources such as the [Visual Arts Data Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_Arts_Data_Service "Visual Arts Data Service") (VADS),[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-125) and [Google Art Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Art_Project "Google Art Project").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-126) In 2012 the museum reported the total size of its art collection as 84,980 items.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwm2012p62-113)

### Film

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Film")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/The_Battle_of_the_Somme_film_image1.jpg/500px-The_Battle_of_the_Somme_film_image1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Battle_of_the_Somme_film_image1.jpg)

A still from the 1916 documentary and propaganda film [_The Battle of the Somme_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Battle_of_the_Somme_(film) "The Battle of the Somme (film)"), preserved by the museum's film archive

The museum's Film and Video Archive is one of the oldest [film archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_archives "Film archives") in the world.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-127)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-128)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-129) The archive preserves a range of historically significant film and video material, including the official British film record of the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). Notable among the archive's First World War holdings is [_The Battle of the Somme_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Battle_of_the_Somme_(film) "The Battle of the Somme (film)"), a pioneering 1916 documentary film (which was inscribed on the [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")[Memory of the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_of_the_World "Memory of the World") register in 2005), and _Der Magische Gürtel_, a German 1917 propaganda film about the submarine [_U-35_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SM_U-35_(Germany) "SM U-35 (Germany)").[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-130) The archive's Second World War holdings include unedited film shot by British military cameramen, which document combat actions such as the British landings on D-Day in June 1944,[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-131) and the liberation of the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in April 1945.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-132)

The archive also holds government information films and propaganda features such as _[Target for Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target\_for\_Tonight "Target for Tonight")_ (1941) and _[Desert Victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert\_Victory "Desert Victory")_ (1943). The archive's post-Second World War collections include material from the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War"), Cold War material, the former film library of [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO"), and material produced by the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") UNTV service in Bosnia. As an official repository under the 1958 Public Records Act, the archive continues to receive material from the Ministry of Defence. The archive also seeks to acquire amateur film taken by both service personnel and civilian cameramen.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-133) Material from the collection was used in the production of TV documentary series such as [_The Great War_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_War_(documentary) "The Great War (documentary)") and _[The World at War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_World\_at\_War "The World at War")_. In 2012 the museum reported the size of its film archive as being in excess of 23,000 hours of film, video and digital footage.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwm2012p62-113) IWM participated in the national digitising project [Unlocking Film Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unlocking_Film_Heritage "Unlocking Film Heritage").

### Photographs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Photographs")]

The museum's Photograph Archive preserves photographs by official, amateur and professional photographers. The collection includes the official British photographic record of the two world wars; the First World War collection includes the work of photographers such as [Ernest Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Brooks_(photographer) "Ernest Brooks (photographer)") and [John Warwick Brooke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Warwick_Brooke?action=edit&redlink=1 "John Warwick Brooke (page does not exist)").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-134)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-135) The archive also holds 150,000 British [aerial photographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerial_photography "Aerial photography") from the First World War,[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-136) the largest collection of its kind.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-137) The Second World War collection includes the work of photographers such as [Bill Brandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Brandt "Bill Brandt"), [Cecil Beaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Beaton "Cecil Beaton")[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-138) and [Bert Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bert_Hardy "Bert Hardy").[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-139) Like the Film Archive, the Photograph Archive is an official repository under the 1958 Public Records Act, and as such continues to receive material from the Ministry of Defence. In 2012 the museum reported the size of its photographic holdings as approximately 11 million images in 17,263 collections.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwm2012p62-113)

### Exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Exhibits")]

The museum's exhibits collection includes a wide range of objects, organised into numerous smaller collections such as uniforms, badges, insignia and flags (including a [Canadian Red Ensign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Red_Ensign "Canadian Red Ensign") carried at [Vimy Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vimy_Ridge "Battle of Vimy Ridge") in 1917,[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-140) a [Union Flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Flag "Union Flag") from the 1942 [British surrender of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Singapore "Battle of Singapore"),[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-141) and another found among the wreckage of the [World Trade Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Center_(1973%E2%80%932001) "World Trade Center (1973–2001)") following the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks")), as well a piece of the towers;[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-142) personal mementoes, souvenirs and miscellanea such as [trench art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trench_art "Trench art");[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-143)[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-144) orders, medals and decorations (including collections of [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Cross "Victoria Cross") and [George Crosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cross "George Cross")); military equipment; firearms and ammunition, ordnance, edged weapons, clubs (such as [trench clubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trench_raiding_club "Trench raiding club"))[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-145) and other weapons, and vehicles, aircraft and ships. The museum holds the national collection of modern firearms.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwm2012p62-113) The firearms collection includes a rifle used by [T. E. Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._E._Lawrence "T. E. Lawrence"),[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-146) and an automatic pistol owned by [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill").[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-147)

The ordnance collection includes artillery pieces that participated in notable battles, such as the Néry gun, a field gun that was used during the 1914 [action at Néry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_at_N%C3%A9ry "Action at Néry"),[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-148) and equipment captured from enemy forces. The museum's vehicles collection includes [_Ole Bill_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGOC_B-type#Ole_Bill "LGOC B-type"), a bus used by British forces in the First World War,[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-149) and a number of vehicles used by [Field Marshal Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Law_Montgomery,_1st_Viscount_Montgomery_of_Alamein "Bernard Law Montgomery, 1st Viscount Montgomery of Alamein") during the Second World War.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-150) The museum's aircraft collection includes aircraft that are notable for their rarity, such as the only complete and original [Royal Aircraft Factory R.E.8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Aircraft_Factory_R.E.8 "Royal Aircraft Factory R.E.8") in existence and one of only two surviving [TSR-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAC_TSR-2 "BAC TSR-2") strike aircraft,[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-R.E.8_Restoration-151)[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-152) and aircraft associated with particular actions, such as a [Supermarine Spitfire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermarine_Spitfire "Supermarine Spitfire") flown during the [Battle of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain "Battle of Britain"). The museum's naval collection includes [HM Coastal Motor Boat 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HM_Coastal_Motor_Boat_4 "HM Coastal Motor Boat 4") and a [midget submarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midget_submarine "Midget submarine")[HMS _XE8_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XE_class_submarine "XE class submarine").[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-153)[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-154) In 2012 the museum reported its exhibits collection to contain 155,000 objects and a further 357 vehicles and aircraft.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwm2012p62-113)

### Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Library")]

The museum's library is a national reference collection on modern conflict, and holds works on all aspects of warfare, including regimental or unit histories (such as 789 rare German unit histories from the First World War),[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-copac-155) technical manuals, biographical material and works on war's social, cultural, economic, political and military aspects. The library also holds printed ephemera such as the [Imperial War Museum Stamp Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_Stamp_Collection "Imperial War Museum Stamp Collection"),[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-stampcollection-156) leaflets and ration books, printed proclamations, newspapers, trench magazines (such _[The Wipers Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wipers\_Times "The Wipers Times")_) and [trench maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trench_map "Trench map").[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-copac-155) In 2012 the museum reported its library collection to contain over 80,000 items of historic importance (such as maps, proclamations and rare books) and a further 254,000 items of reference material.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwm2012p62-113)

### Sound

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Sound")]

The museum's Sound Archive holds 33,000 sound recordings, including a large collection of [oral history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_history "Oral history") recordings of witnesses to conflicts since 1914.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwmsounnd-157) The museum's sound collection originated in 1972 with the creation of the Department of Sound Records and the instigation of an oral history recording programme. The sound collection opened to the public in July 1977.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-158) The collection also includes recordings made by the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") during the Second World War, actuality sound effects, broadcasts, speeches and poetry. As part of the museum's First World War centenary programme, the museum is producing _Voices of the First World War_, a [podcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast "Podcast") series drawing upon the museum's oral history recordings.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-159) In 2012 the museum reported the size of its sound collection as 37,000 hours.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwm2012p62-113)

### Databases

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Databases")]

The IWM has an online database, listing the various items which make up the IWM Collections. In some cases, there are images of the item, or contemporary photos, which can be shared and reused under a [Creative Commons Licence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Commons_license "Creative Commons license").

The [War Memorials Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Memorials_Register "War Memorials Register") is a database of known [war memorials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_memorial "War memorial") in the United Kingdom. Information such as the material used in construction, the condition of the memorial, its address and coordinates with a satellite map plot are recorded for each of the memorials. Whilst many memorials commemorate those who died in the First World War,[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-160) the scope of the project is all conflicts. As of 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit), there are over 90,000 memorials on the register.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-161)

In 2014, IWM and online genealogy service provider [Findmypast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Findmypast "Findmypast") entered into a collaboration to launch the "**Lives of the First World War**" platform.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-162) During the centenary period, anyone could sign up for an account, and those who paid for a subscription had the ability to add records from Findmypast's collections.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-family-tree-163)

A number of sources (War Office medal index cards, Canadian Expeditionary Force attestations, Royal Navy service records etc.) had been used as seeding documents to create individual entries in the database. Each person's profile in the database could have been further built up, so as to document when that person was born, when they died, family members etc. If a person needed to be added, or a duplicate existed that needed to be merged, such activity was requested via a support forum handled by IWM volunteers. A user with a subscription had the ability to group person profiles together into a "community". This could be a grouping based around a ship's crew, a unit in the army, or the names of men and women buried in a given war cemetery.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-LivesKB-164)

The goal was to encourage [crowdsourcing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crowdsourcing "Crowdsourcing") to build up as many details as possible in the database, and to tap into the popularity of online genealogy as a pastime. One selling point of the platform was that the data thus captured would form a "permanent digital memorial[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-165) [that] will be saved for future generations."[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Lives-166) The IWM declared that the data from the platform would become part of its archive when the platform ceased to be interactive in 2019, "and will be free to access online for research."[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Lives_legacy-167)

### Size of collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Size of collection")]

The museum holds around half a [petabyte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petabyte "Petabyte") of digitised data (as of 2017). This is held in [Duxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duxford "Duxford") (Cambridgeshire) on two SpectraLogic T950 tape libraries, with a distance of 500m between them. One is a LTO-5 ([Linear Tape-Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_Tape-Open "Linear Tape-Open")) tape library, the other is IBM [TS1150](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_3592 "IBM 3592").[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-168)

The **Imperial War Museum** (**IWM**), currently branded "**Imperial War Museums**", is a British [national museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_museum "National museum"). Its headquarters are in London, with five branches in England. Founded as the Imperial War Museum in 1917, it was intended to record the civil and military war effort and sacrifice of the United Kingdom and [its Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") during the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"). The museum's remit has since expanded to include all conflicts in which British or Commonwealth forces have been involved since 1914. As of 2012, the museum aims "to provide for, and to encourage, the study and understanding of the history of modern war and 'wartime experience'."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-3)

Originally housed in [the Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace") at [Sydenham Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydenham_Hill "Sydenham Hill"), the museum opened to the public in 1920. In 1924, it moved to space in the [Imperial Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Institute "Imperial Institute") in [South Kensington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Kensington "South Kensington") and in 1936 it acquired a permanent home at the former [Bethlem Royal Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlem_Royal_Hospital "Bethlem Royal Hospital") in [Southwark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwark "Southwark"), which serves as its headquarters. The outbreak of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") saw the museum expand both its collections and its terms of reference, but in the post-war period it entered a period of decline. In 1976 the museum opened [IWM Duxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_Duxford "Imperial War Museum Duxford") at [Duxford airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duxford_Aerodrome "Duxford Aerodrome") in [Cambridgeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridgeshire "Cambridgeshire"), and in 1978 the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") cruiser [HMS _Belfast_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Belfast "HMS Belfast"), which is permanently berthed on the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames") in central London, became a branch of the museum. In 1984, [Churchill War Rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_War_Rooms "Cabinet War Rooms"), an underground wartime command centre in [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster "Westminster"), were opened to the public. In 2002 [IWM North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_North "Imperial War Museum North") opened in [Trafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafford "Trafford"), [Greater Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Manchester "Greater Manchester"), the fifth branch of the museum and the first in the north of England. From the 1980s onwards, the museum's Southwark building underwent a series of multimillion-pound redevelopments, the latest of which was completed in 2022.

The museum's collections include [archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archives "Archives") of personal and official documents, [photographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photographs "Photographs"), [film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film "Film") and [video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video "Video") material, and [oral history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_history "Oral history") recordings, an extensive [library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library "Library"), a large [art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art "Art") collection, and examples of military vehicles and aircraft, equipment, and other artefacts.

The museum is funded by government grants, charitable donations, and revenue generation through commercial activity such as retailing, licensing, and publishing. General admission is free to IWM London (although specific exhibitions require the purchase of a ticket) and IWM North, but an admission fee is levied at the other branches. The museum is an [exempt charity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exempt_charity "Exempt charity") under the Charities Act 1993 and a [non-departmental public body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-departmental_public_body "Non-departmental public body") under the [Department for Culture, Media and Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Culture,_Media_and_Sport "Department for Culture, Media and Sport"). As of April 2024, the chairman of the trustees is [Guy Weston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Weston "Guy Weston"). Since May 2023, Caro Howell has served as the museum's director-general.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-4)

## History of the museum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History of the museum")]

### Establishment: 1917–1921

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Establishment: 1917–1921")]

[![Image 9: Head and shoulders shot of a bald, moustached man looking into the camera.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Alfred_Mond.jpg/250px-Alfred_Mond.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alfred_Mond.jpg)

Sir Alfred Mond, photographed between 1910 and 1920

On 27 February 1917 [Sir Alfred Mond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Mond,_1st_Baron_Melchett "Alfred Mond, 1st Baron Melchett"), a Liberal MP and First Commissioner of Works, wrote to the Prime Minister [David Lloyd George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lloyd_George "David Lloyd George") to propose the establishment of a National War Museum. This proposal was accepted by the [War Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_cabinet#United_Kingdom "War cabinet") on 5 March 1917 and the decision announced in _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_ on 26 March. A committee was established, chaired by Mond, to oversee the collection of material to be exhibited in the new museum.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-6)

This National War Museum Committee set about collecting material to illustrate Britain's war effort by dividing into subcommittees examining such subjects as the Army, the Navy, the production of [munitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munitions "Munitions"), and [women's war work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_roles_in_the_World_Wars "Women's roles in the World Wars").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-7) There was an early appreciation of the need for exhibits to reflect personal experience in order to prevent the collections becoming dead relics. [Sir Martin Conway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Conway,_1st_Baron_Conway_of_Allington "Martin Conway, 1st Baron Conway of Allington"), the museum's first director-general, said that exhibits must "be vitalised by contributions expressive of the action, the experiences, the valour and the endurance of individuals".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-8) The museum's first [curator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curator "Curator") and secretary was [Charles ffoulkes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_ffoulkes "Charles ffoulkes"), who had previously been curator of the [Royal Armouries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Armouries "Royal Armouries") at the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London "Tower of London").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-9) In July 1917 Mond made a visit to the [Western Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Front_(World_War_I) "Western Front (World War I)") in order to study how best to organise the museum's growing collection. While in France he met French government ministers, along with Field Marshal [Sir Douglas Haig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Haig,_1st_Earl_Haig "Douglas Haig, 1st Earl Haig"), [Commander-in-Chief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander-in-chief "Commander-in-chief") (C-in-C) of the [British Expeditionary Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Expeditionary_Force_(World_War_I) "British Expeditionary Force (World War I)") (BEF) on the Western Front, who reportedly took great interest in his work.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-10) In December 1917 the name was changed to the _Imperial_ War Museum after a resolution from the India and Dominions Committee of the museum.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-11)

The museum was opened by King [George V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_V "George V") at [the Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace") on 9 June 1920. During the opening ceremony, Sir Alfred Mond addressed the King on behalf of the committee, saying that "it was hoped to make the museum so complete that every one who took part in the war, however obscurely, would find therein an example or illustration of the sacrifice he or she made" and that the museum "was not a monument of military glory, but a record of toil and sacrifice".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-14) Shortly afterwards the **Imperial War Museum Act 1920** ([10 & 11 Geo. 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10_&_11_Geo._5 "10 & 11 Geo. 5"). c. 16) was passed and established a board of trustees to oversee the governance of the museum. To reflect the museum's Imperial remit the board included appointees of the governments of [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-iwm1920-15) While the act was being debated, some [parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Parliament of the United Kingdom") felt that the museum would perpetuate an undesirable war spirit and [Lieutenant-Commander Joseph Kenworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Kenworthy,_10th_Baron_Strabolgi "Joseph Kenworthy, 10th Baron Strabolgi") MP said that he would "refuse to vote a penny of public money to commemorate such suicidal madness of civilisation as that which was shown in the late War".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-16) On the [August Bank Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Bank_Holiday "August Bank Holiday") 1920, the first public holiday since the museum's opening, 94,179 visitors were received,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-tpyf-17) and by November 1921, 2,290,719 had visited the museum.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-18)

In 1924 the museum moved to the [Imperial Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Institute "Imperial Institute") building (demolished in the 1950s and 1960s to make way for [Imperial College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_College "Imperial College")) in South Kensington. While this location was more central and in a prestigious area for museums, the accommodation itself proved cramped and inadequate[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-20) and in 1936 a new permanent location was found south of the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames") in Southwark. The building, designed by [James Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lewis_(architect)?action=edit&redlink=1 "James Lewis (architect) (page does not exist)")[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-21) was the former Bethlem Royal Hospital which had been vacated following the hospital's relocation to Beckenham in Kent. The site was owned by [Lord Rothermere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Harmsworth,_1st_Viscount_Rothermere "Harold Harmsworth, 1st Viscount Rothermere"), who had originally intended to demolish the building to provide a public park in what was a severely overcrowded area of London. Eventually the central portion of the hospital building was retained.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-:0-22)

The two extensive wings were removed and the resulting space named [Geraldine Mary Harmsworth Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_Mary_Harmsworth_Park "Geraldine Mary Harmsworth Park"), after Lord Rothermere's mother. Sir Martin Conway described the building as "...a fine building, really quite noble building, with a great portico, a distinguishing dome, and two great wings added to it for the accommodation of lunatics no longer required. This particular building can be made to contain our collection admirably, and we shall preserve from destruction quite a fine building which otherwise will disappear".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-:0-22) The "distinguishing dome" was added by [Sydney Smirke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Smirke "Sydney Smirke") in 1846 and housed the hospital's chapel.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-23) The museum was reopened by the Duke of York (later [King George VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_George_VI "King George VI")) in its new accommodation on 7 July 1936.

### Second World War and after: 1939–1966

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Second World War and after: 1939–1966")]

With the outbreak of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") in 1939, the museum began to collect material documenting the conflict.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-24) In November 1939, during the "[Phoney War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoney_War "Phoney War")", the museum appeared in the opening sequence of the [GPO Film Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPO_Film_Unit "GPO Film Unit") production _The First Days_, in which children are seen playing on some of the museum's German artillery pieces captured during the First World War.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-25) With the [Dunkirk evacuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkirk_evacuation "Dunkirk evacuation") in May–June 1940, the British Army's shortage of equipment saw eighteen of the museum's artillery pieces return to military service.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-charman103-26) The museum's trench clubs were used by the [Home Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Guard_(United_Kingdom) "Home Guard (United Kingdom)"), while other items such as sights and optical instruments were returned to the Ministry of Supply. The museum refused to return some historic items such as a naval gun from [HMS _Lance_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Lance_(1914) "HMS Lance (1914)") (which had fired Britain's first shot of the First World War) or a gun served by [Victoria Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Cross "Victoria Cross")-winning boy seaman [Jack Cornwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Cornwell "Jack Cornwell").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-charman103-26) The museum was closed for the duration of the war in September 1940 with the onset of [the Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blitz "The Blitz"). On 31 January 1941 the museum was struck by a _[Luftwaffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luftwaffe "Luftwaffe")_ bomb which fell on the naval gallery. A number of ship models were damaged by the blast and a [Short Type 184](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_Type_184 "Short Type 184") seaplane, which had flown at the [Battle of Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Jutland "Battle of Jutland"), was destroyed.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-IWMLguide2-27) While closed to the public the museum's building was used for a variety of purposes connected to the war effort, such as a repair garage for government motor vehicles, a centre for Air Raid Precautions civil defence lectures and a fire fighting training school.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-28)

In October 1945 the museum mounted a temporary exhibition, the first since the end of the war in August, which showcased technologies developed by the [Petroleum Warfare Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_Warfare_Department "Petroleum Warfare Department"). These included the submarine fuel pipeline [PLUTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Pluto "Operation Pluto"), the fog dispersal method [FIDO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog_Investigation_and_Dispersal_Operation "Fog Investigation and Dispersal Operation"), and flame weapons such as the [Churchill Crocodile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Churchill_Crocodile "Churchill Crocodile") and Wasp [Universal Carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Carrier "Universal Carrier").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-29) Due to bomb damage to the building and exhibits, the museum was obliged to reopen its galleries piecemeal and opened a portion of its galleries in November 1946.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-IWMLguide2-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Imperial_War_Museum_page_7-30) A third of the galleries were opened in 1948 and a further wing opened in 1949.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-31)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-32) In 1953, with Commonwealth forces engaged in [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War") and [Malaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayan_Emergency "Malayan Emergency") the museum began its current policy of collecting material from all modern conflicts in which British or Commonwealth forces were involved.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-IWMLguide2-27) Despite this expansion of remit, the early postwar period was a period of decline for the museum. [Noble Frankland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_Frankland "Noble Frankland"), the museum's director from 1960 to 1982, described the museum's galleries in 1955 as appearing "dingy and neglected [and in a] dismal state of decay" the museum's "numerous stunning exhibits" notwithstanding.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-33)

### Redevelopment and expansion: 1966–2012

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Imperial_War_Museum&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Redevelopment and expansion: 1966–2012")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/15inchgunsatImperialWarMuseumLondon.jpg/250px-15inchgunsatImperialWarMuseumLondon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:15inchgunsatImperialWarMuseumLondon.jpg)

15-inch guns outside the museum; the nearer gun from [HMS _Ramillies_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Ramillies_(07) "HMS Ramillies (07)"), the other from [HMS _Resolution_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Resolution_(09) "HMS Resolution (09)")

In 1966 the museum's Southwark building was extended to provide collections storage and other facilities, the first major expansion since the museum had moved to the site. The development also included a purpose-built cinema.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-34) In 1967 the museum acquired a pair of [15-inch naval guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BL_15-inch_Mk_I_naval_gun "BL 15-inch Mk I naval gun"). One had been mounted on the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy")'s [HMS _Ramillies_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Ramillies_(07) "HMS Ramillies (07)") and the other on both [HMS _Resolution_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Resolution_(09) "HMS Resolution (09)") and [HMS _Roberts_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Roberts_(F40) "HMS Roberts (F40)"). Both had been fired in action during the Second World War. They went on permanent display outside the museum in May 1968.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-35) The acquisition of these guns, representative of the [dreadnought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreadnought "Dreadnought") era of British [battleships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship "Battleship"), led the museum to seek to acquire a [6-inch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BL_6-inch_Mk_XXIII_naval_gun "BL 6-inch Mk XXIII naval gun") triple turret that would be representative of a number of classes of British [cruisers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruiser "Cruiser").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Wingate101-36) This would eventually lead to the preservation of the Royal Navy [light cruiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_cruiser "Light cruiser")[HMS _Belfast_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Belfast "HMS Belfast"), which became a branch of the museum in 1978.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-37) Later in 1968 on 13 October the museum was attacked by an [arsonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsonist "Arsonist"), Timothy John Daly, who claimed he was acting in protest against the exhibition of [militarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Militarism "Militarism") to children. He caused damage valued at approximately £200,000, not counting the loss of irreplaceable books and documents. On his conviction in 1969 he was sentenced to four years in prison.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-38)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-39)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/V-1_flying_bomb_on_display_at_Imperial_War_Museum.jpg/250px-V-1_flying_bomb_on_display_at_Imperial_War_Museum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:V-1_flying_bomb_on_display_at_Imperial_War_Museum.jpg)

[V-1 flying bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V-1_flying_bomb "V-1 flying bomb") on display

In 1969 RAF Duxford, a [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") fighter airfield in [Cambridgeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridgeshire "Cambridgeshire") was declared surplus to requirements by the [Ministry of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_(United_Kingdom) "Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)"). Needing further space, the museum duly requested permission to use part of the site as temporary storage. The entire site was later transferred to the museum in February 1976 and Duxford, now referred to as [Imperial War Museum Duxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum_Duxford "Imperial War Museum Duxford") became the museum's first branch.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Frankland-40) Also during the 1970s the government raised the possibility of the museum taking over the historic [Cabinet War Rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_War_Rooms "Cabinet War Rooms") in [Whitehall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehall "Whitehall"). The museum was reluctant due to its new commitments related to Duxford and HMS _Belfast_, but agreed in 1982.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-Holmes-41)

By 1983 the museum was again looking to redevelop the Southwark site and approached engineering firm [Arup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arup_Group "Arup Group") to plan a phased programme of works that would expand the building's exhibition space, provide appropriate environmental controls to protect collections, and improve facilities for visitors. The following year, in April 1984, the Cabinet War Rooms were opened to the public as a branch of the museum.

The first phase of the works to the Southwark building started in 1986 and were completed in 1989, during which time the museum was closed to the public. The work included the conversion of what was previously the hospital's courtyard into a centrepiece Large Exhibits Gallery. This gallery featured a strengthened ground floor (to support the weight of very heavy exhibits), a first floor [mezzanine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mezzanine_(architecture) "Mezzanine (architecture)") and second storey viewing balcony. Into this space were placed tanks, artillery pieces, vehicles, ordnance and aircraft from the First World War to the [Falklands War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falklands_War "Falklands War").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-arupjournal-42) For some years the museum was marketed as "The _new_ Imperial War Museum".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-43) This atrium, with its concentration of military hardware, has been described as "the biggest boys' bedroom in London".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-44) This first phase cost £16.7 million (of which £12 million was provided by the government) and the museum was reopened by [The Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") on 29 June 1989.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-45) In 1990, the museum was awarded National Heritage [Museum of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_the_Year "Museum of the Year").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_War_Museum#cite_note-46)
